docs.title: Big Data Analytics with Python
docs.text: A Masters course at the African Institute for Mathematical Sciences (AIMS) Rwanda. We start from the question "why does my laptop crash on this file?" and finish with distributed machine learning, streaming pipelines and satellite analytics on real African data.

docs.title: How the course is built
docs.text:
Every chapter follows the same rhythm, so you always know where you are:

  1. Concepts — the theory and the mathematics, explained with pictures and small examples.
  2. Code — runnable Python you can paste into Jupyter or Google Colab.
  3. Lab — a guided exercise on a real dataset (30–90 minutes).
  4. Check yourself — review questions, some with hidden answers.

docs.title: The learning path
docs.text:
Foundations Chapters 1–3: what makes data "big", making Python fast, and storing data well

Scaling out Chapters 4–7: MapReduce, Polars, DuckDB, Dask and Apache Spark

Analytics at scale Chapters 8–11: machine learning, streaming, geospatial, text and graphs

Production & responsibility Chapters 12–13: pipelines, cloud, ethics and Rwanda's data protection law

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:

No powerful laptop? No problem.

Every lab can run on Google Colab (free) or the Databricks Free Edition. Chapters note where a dataset should be subsampled for a modest machine.

docs.title: Course description
docs.text: This course equips Masters students with the theory and practical skills needed to store, process, analyse and model datasets that exceed the capacity of a single computer's memory — or that arrive too fast to process with traditional tools. Students learn the principles of distributed computing, modern columnar storage, and the Python big data ecosystem (PyArrow, Polars, DuckDB, Dask, PySpark), then apply them to machine learning, streaming, geospatial and text analytics on real datasets, with an emphasis on African and Rwandan data.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

  1. Explain the defining characteristics of big data and the trade-offs of distributed systems (scale-up vs scale-out, CAP theorem, Amdahl's law, data locality).
  2. Diagnose the performance and memory behaviour of Python data code and choose an appropriate tool for a given data size.
  3. Design storage layouts using columnar formats (Parquet), partitioning and table formats (Delta Lake / Apache Iceberg).
  4. Implement analytics with the MapReduce model and with Apache Spark (DataFrames, SQL, RDDs), and tune Spark jobs by reading query plans.
  5. Build scalable machine learning pipelines with Spark MLlib and Dask.
  6. Process real-time data streams with windowing and watermarks.
  7. Analyse large geospatial, raster, text and graph datasets.
  8. Evaluate the ethical, legal and privacy implications of big data projects, including Rwanda's Law No. 058/2021 on the protection of personal data and privacy.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python programming (functions, classes, comprehensions), pandas and NumPy.
  • Probability, statistics and introductory machine learning (regression, classification, evaluation).
  • Basic command line use. Git is recommended (it is reviewed in the setup guide).

docs.title: Policies
docs.text:
• Collaboration. Discussing ideas is encouraged; code and reports you submit must be your own (or your group's, for the capstone). Cite any source you adapt, including AI assistants — state what you used them for.
  • Reproducibility. Every submission is a Git repository with a README.md, an environment file (requirements.txt or environment.yml) and instructions that let the instructor re-run your work.
  • Compute fairness. Assignments are designed to run on a laptop with 8 GB RAM, Google Colab, or Databricks Free Edition. Larger-scale runs are welcome but never required.

docs.text:
There are five individual assignments and one group capstone. Each assignment is released after the relevant chapters and gives students about four days in an intensive block (or two weeks in a semester).

docs.text:
Every submission is a GitHub repository (private, shared with the instructor, or via GitHub Classroom) containing:

docs.title: Common rubric
docs.text: Criterion Excellent (90–100%) Good (70–89%) Adequate (50–69%) Insufficient (<50%) Correctness (35%) All tasks correct, results validated against independent checks Minor errors Some tasks incorrect or unvalidated Major errors or missing tasks Scalability reasoning (25%) Choices justified with measurements (time, memory, plans, Spark UI); trade-offs discussed Sensible choices, some measurement Works but no justification Approach would not scale; no awareness Code quality & reproducibility (20%) Clean, modular, documented; runs from README in one go Mostly reproducible Hard to run; hard-coded paths Cannot be run Communication (20%) Clear report, good figures, honest limitations, actionable conclusions Clear but thin discussion Results without interpretation Unclear or missing report

docs.title: Use of AI assistants
docs.text: AI assistants may be used for help with syntax, debugging and explanations. Students must (1) state in the README what they used them for, (2) be able to explain every line of code in an oral check, and (3) never submit generated text as their own analysis without verification. Results that cannot be reproduced score zero for correctness.

docs.title: Late policy and compute problems
docs.text: Power cuts and connectivity problems are real. If a dataset download or cloud job fails, document what happened and submit results on a documented subset; partial credit is given for sound reasoning on smaller data. Contact the instructor or tutors before the deadline, not after.

docs.title: A1 — Formats & single-node engines
docs.text: Chapters: 1, 2, 3, 5 · Dataset: NYC TLC yellow taxi trips, 12 months (≈ 40 million rows) · Effort: ~12 hours

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Demonstrate, with measurements, how storage format, data types and engine choice change what a single machine can do.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Estimate before loading (10%). Using file metadata only (PyArrow footers), report the row count, columns and compressed size of the 12 files. Estimate the in-memory size in pandas with default dtypes. Explain your calculation.
  2. Format benchmark (25%). For one month, write CSV, CSV.gz, Parquet (snappy, zstd) and Feather. Measure file size, write time, full read time and 2-column read time. Present a table and a short explanation grounded in Chapter 3.
  3. Dtypes (15%). Load one month in pandas with defaults, then with optimised dtypes and usecols. Report memory reduction per column.
  4. Partitioning (15%). Write all 12 months as a Hive-partitioned dataset (year, month). Show partition pruning by timing a single-month query versus a full scan. Then show the small files problem with a bad partitioning choice.
  5. Three engines (25%). Answer the question: "For each pickup borough and hour of day, what are the median fare per mile and the share of trips paid by card?" in Polars (lazy, streaming), DuckDB and Dask, over all 12 months. Report time and peak memory; include the query plans showing projection and predicate pushdown.
  6. Recommendation (10%). In half a page, recommend a tool and storage layout for a team that will receive one new month each month and run this kind of query daily.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Your three engines must agree (to rounding). Include the check in your notebook.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Repeat task 5 directly over HTTP with DuckDB without downloading the files.
  • Sort data by pickup time before writing, and show the effect on row-group skipping.

docs.title: A2 — MapReduce & Spark at scale
docs.text: Chapters: 4, 6, 7 · Dataset: Wikipedia hourly pageviews, 7 consecutive days (~168 files, ~8 GB compressed) · Effort: ~15 hours

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Implement the same analysis with your own MapReduce engine and with Spark; then optimise the Spark job using query plans and the Spark UI.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. MapReduce by hand (20%). Using minimr.py from Chapter 4 on one day of data: compute total views per language edition (domain_code prefix). Use a correct combiner. Report the number of intermediate pairs with and without the combiner.
  2. Spark ingestion (15%). Read all 7 days with an explicit schema. Extract date and hour from file names. Write as Parquet partitioned by date. Report raw versus Parquet sizes.
  3. Analysis (30%).
    1. Top 25 pages per day for rw, sw, fr and en Wikipedia (excluding Main_Page, Special: pages and similar).
    2. Using window functions: the 20 English pages with the largest day-over-day relative increase (minimum 10,000 views on the later day). Identify the events behind three of them.
    3. Hour-of-day profile of total views for 5 languages of your choice, normalised to each language's daily total. Interpret differences in time zones.
  4. Optimisation (25%). Take your slowest query. Show explain("formatted") and Spark UI screenshots before and after at least two optimisations (e.g., broadcast join, partition pruning, avoiding a UDF, adjusting shuffle partitions, caching). Quantify the improvement.
  5. Reflection (10%). Compare writing the analysis in MapReduce versus Spark: lines of code, run time, ease of reasoning.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• If 7 days is too large for your machine, use 3 days and say so; the grading focuses on method.
  • On Databricks Free Edition, upload a subset to a volume or read via the URL with a download step.

docs.title: A3 — Machine learning at scale
docs.text: Chapter: 8 · Dataset (choose one): NYC TLC trips (3+ months) or Amazon Reviews 2023 (one or more large categories) · Effort: ~15 hours

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Build, evaluate and justify a scalable ML pipeline, and determine whether "more data" actually helps.

docs.title: Option A — Taxi trip duration (regression)
docs.text: Predict trip duration in minutes at pickup time (features available at pickup only: zones, time, distance estimate, etc.).

docs.title: Option B — Review sentiment (classification)
docs.text: Predict whether a review is positive (4–5 stars) from text, using Spark ML text features.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Problem framing (10%). Define the target, the prediction moment, and list features that would leak. Choose metrics and justify them.
  2. Feature pipeline (20%). Build a Spark ML Pipeline with appropriate transformers. Use a split that respects time (Option A) or product/user grouping (Option B).
  3. Model comparison (20%). Train at least three models (e.g., linear/logistic, random forest, GBT). Report metrics and training time.
  4. Learning curve (20%). Train your best model on 0.1%, 1%, 10% and 100% of the training data. Plot validation metric and training time versus size. Is distributed training justified?
  5. Tuning (15%). Tune two hyperparameters with TrainValidationSplit on a sample; refit on all data. Discuss the cost of tuning at scale.
  6. Scoring and analysis (15%). Score the full test set. Analyse errors by subgroup (borough/hour, or product category). Persist and reload the model.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Train a scikit-learn or LightGBM model on a sample and score the full data with a pandas UDF; compare with MLlib.
  • applyInPandas: one model per borough or category; compare with the global model.

docs.title: A4 — Streaming analytics
docs.text: Chapter: 9 · Dataset: Wikimedia EventStreams (live) — or synthetic mobile money via Kafka · Effort: ~12 hours

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Build a fault-tolerant streaming application with event-time windows, watermarks and a reliable sink, and show you understand its guarantees.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Ingestion (15%). Bridge the live stream into Spark (file drop as in Chapter 9, or Kafka). Run for at least 30 minutes and keep the raw events.
  2. Windowed metrics (25%). Every minute, for each wiki: number of edits, share by bots, approximate distinct editors (approx_count_distinct), and mean absolute size change (length.new − length.old, where available). Use event time with a watermark you justify.
  3. Alerting (20%). Detect "edit bursts": a page with ≥ 5 edits from ≥ 3 distinct users within 10 minutes. Write alerts to a separate sink.
  4. Fault tolerance (20%). Write raw events to Parquet (or Delta) with checkpointing. Kill the query mid-run and restart it. Prove there are no lost or duplicated events (e.g., by event id / meta.id).
  5. Sketches (10%). Implement reservoir sampling and a Count-Min Sketch in Python on the raw events; compare the sketch's top-20 page estimates with exact counts.
  6. Report (10%). Explain your output mode choices, watermark trade-offs, latency observed (lastProgress), and what would change for a production mobile money fraud system.

docs.title: Alternative: synthetic mobile money
docs.text: Use the Faker generator from Data sources with Kafka (docker compose in labs/). Inject delayed events (10% arrive 1–30 minutes late) and show how your watermark handles them.

docs.title: A5 — Geospatial big data for Rwanda
docs.text: Chapter: 10 · Datasets: CHIRPS daily rainfall, Google Open Buildings (Rwanda), WorldPop population, geoBoundaries districts/sectors · Effort: ~15 hours

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Combine raster and vector big data to produce decision-relevant indicators for Rwanda at district and H3 levels.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Rainfall climatology (25%). With xarray + Dask, compute Season A (Sep–Dec) and Season B (Mar–May) rainfall totals per year (at least 20 years) for each district. Map the long-term mean and the coefficient of variation.
  2. Drought years (15%). Compute standardised anomalies per district and season. Identify the three worst seasons in the record and check whether they match known events (cite sources).
  3. Built environment (25%). Aggregate Open Buildings (confidence ≥ 0.75) to H3 resolution 7 with DuckDB or Spark: building count and built area per cell. Join with WorldPop aggregated to the same cells.
  4. Integrated indicator (20%). Construct an indicator combining population exposure and rainfall variability (justify its form). Map it at H3 resolution 7 and summarise per district.
  5. Performance & limitations (15%). Report run times and memory; explain chunking choices. Discuss data quality: building detection errors, population model assumptions, CHIRPS accuracy in mountainous terrain.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Clip rasters to Rwanda's bounding box early to reduce data.
  • Use EPSG:32735 for area calculations.
  • If bandwidth is limited, use CHIRPS monthly files instead of daily for task 1.

docs.title: 1. What is big data?
docs.text:
Learning objectives

After this chapter you can:

  • define big data operationally, rather than by a fixed size threshold;
  • describe the 5 Vs and give an African example of each;
  • estimate the memory and time cost of a dataset before you load it;
  • explain why we scale out (more machines) instead of only scaling up (a bigger machine);
  • place the tools of this course on a map of data size versus complexity.

docs.title: 1.1 A working definition
docs.text:
There is no magic number of gigabytes at which data becomes "big". A useful, operational definition is:

Data is "big" when the way you have been processing it stops working — it no longer fits in memory, takes too long, arrives too fast, or is too varied for your current tools — and you must change your architecture, not just your code.

For a pandas user on an 8 GB laptop, a 5 GB CSV is big data. For a bank, it may be 50 TB of transactions. The principles are the same; the course teaches you to recognise the moment you cross the line and to choose the right next tool.

docs.title: 1.2 The 5 Vs
docs.text:
V Meaning African / Rwandan example Volume Amount of data Sentinel-2 satellite imagery of Africa: petabytes, updated every 5 days Velocity Speed of arrival and required response time Mobile money transactions: MTN MoMo and Airtel Money process millions per day; fraud must be flagged in milliseconds Variety Diversity of structure A health ministry combining DHIS2 tables, scanned forms, SMS reports and GPS of clinics Veracity Quality and trustworthiness Crowd-sourced OpenStreetMap roads; sensor readings with gaps during power cuts Value Usefulness for decisions Rainfall forecasts that change when farmers plant beans in Rwanda's Season A

Some authors add Variability (meaning changes over time — e.g., the word "airtime" in text) and Visualisation. Do not memorise lists; ask instead which V is making your problem hard, because each V calls for a different solution:

  • Volume → distributed storage and computation (Chapters 3–7).
  • Velocity → stream processing (Chapter 9).
  • Variety → schema-on-read, data lakes, flexible formats (Chapter 3).
  • Veracity → validation, data quality pipelines (Chapter 12).
  • Value → good questions, sound statistics, ethics (Chapters 8 and 13).

docs.title: 1.3 Back-of-the-envelope estimation
docs.text:
Good data engineers estimate before they compute. Memorise these orders of magnitude:

Unit Bytes Intuition 1 KB \(10^3\) A short text message record 1 MB \(10^6\) A photo 1 GB \(10^9\) One month of NYC yellow-taxi trips as Parquet is ~50 MB; as CSV ~500 MB 1 TB \(10^{12}\) A large laptop disk 1 PB \(10^{15}\) Large satellite archives

And these approximate latencies (the "numbers every programmer should know", rounded):

Operation Time Read from L1 CPU cache ~1 ns Read from RAM ~100 ns Read 1 MB sequentially from RAM ~10 µs Read 1 MB sequentially from SSD ~200 µs–1 ms Read 1 MB sequentially from spinning disk ~5 ms Network round trip within a datacentre ~0.5 ms Network round trip Kigali ↔ Europe ~100–150 ms

Lesson: RAM is roughly 10–100× faster than disk, and disk is far faster than the wide-area network. Big data systems are designed around moving computation to the data, not data to the computation.

docs.title: Worked example: will it fit?
docs.text:
A national survey has 12 million rows and 40 columns: 30 float64 columns, 10 string columns averaging 15 characters.

\[ \text{floats: } 12\times10^6 \times 30 \times 8 \text{ B} = 2.88 \text{ GB} \]

pandas stores Python strings with ~50 bytes of object overhead each, so

\[ \text{strings: } 12\times10^6 \times 10 \times (50 + 15) \text{ B} \approx 7.8 \text{ GB} \]

Total ≈ 10.7 GB before any copies made during operations (a merge or groupby can easily double peak memory). On an 8 GB laptop this fails. Chapter 2 shows how to cut it to ~2 GB with better dtypes; Chapter 5 shows how to avoid loading it at all.

def estimate_gb(rows, n_float=0, n_int=0, n_str=0, avg_str_len=10, str_overhead=50):
    """Rough in-memory size of a pandas DataFrame in GB."""
    b = rows * (n_float * 8 + n_int * 8 + n_str * (str_overhead + avg_str_len))
    return b / 1e9

print(f"{estimate_gb(12_000_000, n_float=30, n_str=10, avg_str_len=15):.1f} GB")

docs.title: 1.4 Scaling up versus scaling out
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Workload grows] --> B{Strategy}
    B -->|Scale up / vertical| C[Bigger machine:<br/>more RAM, more cores]
    B -->|Scale out / horizontal| D[More machines<br/>working together]
    C --> E[Simple code<br/>Hard ceiling, expensive at the top]
    D --> F[Near-unlimited capacity<br/>Coordination, network, failures]

Scaling up is underrated: a single modern server with 1 TB of RAM and 128 cores handles a surprising amount of "big" data, and tools like Polars and DuckDB (Chapter 5) exploit it brilliantly. Scaling out becomes necessary when data exceeds what one machine can store or process in acceptable time, or when you need fault tolerance.

docs.title: Amdahl's law — the limit of parallelism
docs.text:
If a fraction \(p\) of a job can be parallelised and the rest \((1-p)\) is serial, the maximum speed-up on \(N\) workers is

\[ S(N) = \frac{1}{(1-p) + \dfrac{p}{N}}, \qquad \lim_{N\to\infty} S(N) = \frac{1}{1-p}. \]

With \(p = 0.95\), even infinitely many machines give at most a 20× speed-up. In big data jobs the serial parts are things like reading a single gzip file, a final sort on one machine, or collecting results to the driver.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

N = np.arange(1, 257)
for p in (0.5, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99):
    plt.plot(N, 1 / ((1 - p) + p / N), label=f"p = {p}")
plt.xscale("log", base=2); plt.xlabel("workers N"); plt.ylabel("speed-up")
plt.legend(); plt.title("Amdahl's law"); plt.show()

Gustafson's law offers the optimistic counterpoint: in practice we use more machines to process more data in the same time, and the parallel fraction grows with the problem size.

docs.text:
Data size (on disk) Typical tool Chapter < 1 GB pandas, NumPy 2 1–100 GB Polars, DuckDB, pandas with chunking, Dask on one machine 2, 5 100 GB – 10 TB Spark or Dask on a cluster; cloud warehouses (BigQuery, Snowflake) 6–8 > 10 TB, or continuous streams Spark / Flink clusters, Kafka, lakehouse tables 3, 9, 12

A brief history helps students see why tools look the way they do:

  • 2003–2004 Google publishes the Google File System and MapReduce papers.
  • 2006 Hadoop (HDFS + MapReduce) brings these ideas to open source.
  • 2010–2014 Spark (UC Berkeley AMPLab) keeps data in memory between steps; becomes an Apache top-level project.
  • 2016+ Apache Arrow standardises in-memory columnar data across languages.
  • 2019+ Lakehouse table formats (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi) bring database guarantees to files in object storage.
  • 2020s Fast single-node engines (DuckDB, Polars) shrink the set of problems that truly need a cluster; Spark 4 adds Spark Connect for thin clients.

docs.title: 2. Python at scale on one machine
docs.text:
Learning objectives

  • Measure time and memory of Python data code instead of guessing.
  • Explain why vectorised NumPy/pandas code is 10–100× faster than loops.
  • Reduce DataFrame memory with dtypes, categoricals and Arrow-backed strings.
  • Process files larger than RAM with chunking and streaming aggregation.
  • Use multiple CPU cores with multiprocessing and concurrent.futures.

Before reaching for a cluster, squeeze your single machine. Many "big data problems" disappear with better dtypes and vectorisation.

docs.title: 2.1 Measure first
docs.text:
"Premature optimisation is the root of all evil." — Donald Knuth

Measure time and memory:

import time, tracemalloc
import numpy as np

def timed(f, *args, repeat=3):
    best = float("inf")
    for _ in range(repeat):
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); f(*args); best = min(best, time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return best

tracemalloc.start()
x = np.random.rand(10_000_000)
current, peak = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
print(f"peak {peak/1e6:.0f} MB")   # ≈ 80 MB = 10M × 8 bytes
tracemalloc.stop()

In Jupyter, use magics: %timeit, %%time, and after %load_ext memory_profiler, %memit.

docs.title: 2.2 Why loops are slow and vectorisation is fast
docs.text:
A Python for loop over a list does, for every element: look up the object, check its type, dispatch the + operator, allocate a new Python object for the result. A NumPy operation runs one compiled C loop over a contiguous block of memory, uses CPU SIMD instructions, and keeps data in cache.

import numpy as np
n = 5_000_000
a = np.random.rand(n); b = np.random.rand(n)
la, lb = a.tolist(), b.tolist()

def py_loop():  return [x * y + 1 for x, y in zip(la, lb)]
def vectorised(): return a * b + 1

print(f"loop       {timed(py_loop):.3f} s")
print(f"vectorised {timed(vectorised):.3f} s")   # typically 50–100× faster

docs.title: Memory layout matters
docs.text: NumPy arrays are contiguous blocks with a fixed dtype. A pandas DataFrame is a collection of columns, each a NumPy (or Arrow) array. Columnar layout means summing one column reads only that column's memory — a theme we will meet again in Parquet (Chapter 3) and Spark (Chapter 6).

docs.title: Avoid apply with Python functions
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"fare": np.random.exponential(15, 2_000_000),
                   "dist": np.random.exponential(3, 2_000_000)})

# Slow: a Python function call per row
%timeit df.apply(lambda r: r.fare / r.dist if r.dist > 0 else np.nan, axis=1)

# Fast: vectorised with np.where
%timeit np.where(df.dist > 0, df.fare / df.dist, np.nan)

When logic truly cannot be vectorised, compile it with Numba:

from numba import njit

@njit
def running_max_drawdown(prices):
    peak = prices[0]; worst = 0.0
    for p in prices:
        peak = max(peak, p)
        worst = min(worst, (p - peak) / peak)
    return worst

docs.title: 2.3 Shrinking DataFrames with dtypes
2.4 Data larger than memory: chunking
docs.text:
The key idea of all big data processing appears here in miniature: process a stream of pieces, keep only small summaries.

from collections import defaultdict

totals = defaultdict(float); counts = defaultdict(int)
for chunk in pd.read_csv("big_trips.csv", chunksize=1_000_000,
                         usecols=["PULocationID", "fare_amount"]):
    g = chunk.groupby("PULocationID")["fare_amount"].agg(["sum", "count"])
    for loc, row in g.iterrows():
        totals[loc] += row["sum"]; counts[loc] += row["count"]

mean_fare = {k: totals[k] / counts[k] for k in totals}

docs.title: Which statistics can be combined across chunks?
docs.text:
A statistic is mergeable (or algebraic) if partial results from chunks combine into the exact global result.

Statistic Mergeable? Partial state to keep count, sum, min, max Yes the value itself mean Yes (sum, count) variance Yes (count, mean, M2) — Welford / Chan median, quantiles Not exactly approximate sketches (t-digest, KLL) distinct count Not exactly HyperLogLog sketch

Parallel variance combination (Chan et al.): for chunks A and B with counts \(n_A, n_B\), means \(\bar x_A, \bar x_B\) and sums of squared deviations \(M_{2,A}, M_{2,B}\):

\[ \delta = \bar x_B - \bar x_A,\quad n = n_A + n_B,\quad \bar x = \bar x_A + \delta\frac{n_B}{n},\quad M_2 = M_{2,A} + M_{2,B} + \delta^2 \frac{n_A n_B}{n}. \] 
def combine(a, b):
    na, ma, m2a = a; nb, mb, m2b = b
    n = na + nb; d = mb - ma
    return n, ma + d * nb / n, m2a + m2b + d * d * na * nb / n

def summarise(x):
    return len(x), x.mean(), ((x - x.mean())**2).sum()

data = np.random.randn(1_000_000) * 3 + 10
state = (0, 0.0, 0.0)
for part in np.array_split(data, 7):
    state = combine(state, summarise(part)) if state[0] else summarise(part)
n, mean, m2 = state
print(mean, m2 / (n - 1), data.var(ddof=1))   # identical

This exact pattern — compute partial states in parallel, then merge — is how Spark and Dask compute aggregations across machines (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 2.5 Using all your cores
docs.text:
Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) means threads do not run Python bytecode in parallel (free-threaded builds of Python 3.13+ are changing this, but most libraries still assume the GIL). Two rules:

  • I/O-bound work (downloads, API calls): use threads — ThreadPoolExecutor.
  • CPU-bound pure-Python work: use processes — ProcessPoolExecutor or multiprocessing.
  • NumPy, Polars, DuckDB and Arrow release the GIL internally and are already multi-threaded.
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor, ThreadPoolExecutor
import glob, urllib.request

# I/O-bound: download 12 months in parallel
months = [f"2024-{m:02d}" for m in range(1, 13)]
def fetch(m):
    url = f"https://d37ci6vzurychx.cloudfront.net/trip-data/yellow_tripdata_{m}.parquet"
    path = f"data/yellow_{m}.parquet"
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, path); return path

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=6) as ex:
    paths = list(ex.map(fetch, months))

# CPU-bound: summarise each file in a separate process
def summarise_file(path):
    d = pd.read_parquet(path, columns=["trip_distance", "fare_amount"])
    return path, len(d), d.fare_amount.sum()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with ProcessPoolExecutor() as ex:
        for path, n, s in ex.map(summarise_file, sorted(glob.glob("data/yellow_*.parquet"))):
            print(path, n, round(s))

Jupyter and multiprocessing

On macOS and Windows, ProcessPoolExecutor needs the worker function to be importable. If it fails in a notebook, put the function in a .py file and import it.

docs.title: 3. Storage, file formats & data lakes
docs.text:
Learning objectives

  • Compare row-oriented and column-oriented storage and know when each wins.
  • Explain how Parquet achieves small files and fast queries (encoding, compression, row groups, statistics).
  • Use Apache Arrow as a zero-copy bridge between tools.
  • Design a partitioned dataset and avoid the "small files problem".
  • Distinguish data warehouses, data lakes and lakehouses; know what Delta Lake and Iceberg add.
  • Recognise the main families of NoSQL databases.

docs.title: 3.1 Row versus column storage
docs.text:
Consider a table of mobile money transactions:

id sender receiver amount district ts

Row-oriented (CSV, JSON lines, Avro, PostgreSQL pages) stores whole records together: 1,A,B,5000,Gasabo,... | 2,C,D,1200,Huye,... | ...

Column-oriented (Parquet, ORC, Arrow, DuckDB, data warehouses) stores each column together: 1,2,3,... | A,C,... | B,D,... | 5000,1200,... | Gasabo,Huye,...

Workload Winner Why Insert/update one transaction (OLTP) Row Write one contiguous record SELECT district, SUM(amount) GROUP BY district over 1 billion rows (OLAP) Column Read 2 of 6 columns; similar values compress well; vectorised CPU loops

Analytics is overwhelmingly OLAP, so big data storage is overwhelmingly columnar.

docs.title: 3.2 Comparing file formats
docs.text:
Format Layout Schema Compression Splittable Typical use CSV Row, text None (inferred) Poor (gzip makes it non-splittable) Yes if uncompressed Exchange, small data JSON / JSON Lines Row, text Self-describing, nested Poor JSONL yes APIs, logs Avro Row, binary Embedded, evolvable Good Yes Kafka messages, write-heavy pipelines Parquet Column, binary Embedded, nested Excellent Yes (row groups) Analytics — the default choice ORC Column, binary Embedded Excellent Yes Hive ecosystems Arrow IPC / Feather Column, binary, in-memory layout Embedded Optional (LZ4/ZSTD) Yes Fast interchange between processes

"Splittable" matters: a 10 GB file that can be split lets 80 workers read it in parallel; a single .csv.gz must be decompressed by one worker from start to end (Amdahl's serial part!).

docs.title: 3.3 Inside Parquet
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    F[Parquet file] --> RG1[Row group 1<br/>~128 MB of rows]
    F --> RG2[Row group 2]
    F --> FT[Footer: schema +<br/>min/max/null stats per column chunk]
    RG1 --> C1[Column chunk: amount<br/>pages, encoded + compressed]
    RG1 --> C2[Column chunk: district]

Four ideas make Parquet fast and small:

  1. Encoding. Dictionary encoding replaces repeated strings ("Gasabo", "Gasabo", "Huye") by small integers plus a dictionary. Run-length encoding stores "Gasabo × 5000". Delta encoding stores differences of sorted timestamps.
  2. Compression on top (Snappy — fast; ZSTD — smaller; GZIP — legacy).
  3. Column pruning (projection pushdown). Read only the requested columns.
  4. Predicate pushdown with statistics. Each column chunk stores min/max. A query WHERE ts >= '2024-06-01' skips row groups whose max timestamp is earlier — without reading them. Sorting data by commonly filtered columns makes this dramatically more effective.
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

pf = pq.ParquetFile("data/yellow_2024_01.parquet")
print(pf.schema_arrow)
print(pf.metadata)                       # rows, row groups, created_by
rg = pf.metadata.row_group(0)
col = rg.column(rg.num_columns - 1)
print(col.path_in_schema, col.compression, col.statistics)

docs.title: Benchmark: CSV versus Parquet
docs.text:
import pandas as pd, time, os

df = pd.read_parquet("data/yellow_2024_01.parquet")
df.to_csv("data/trips.csv", index=False)
for codec in ("snappy", "zstd", "gzip"):
    df.to_parquet(f"data/trips_{codec}.parquet", compression=codec)

for f in ["data/trips.csv", "data/trips_snappy.parquet",
          "data/trips_zstd.parquet", "data/trips_gzip.parquet"]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    if f.endswith(".csv"):
        pd.read_csv(f, usecols=["PULocationID", "fare_amount"])
    else:
        pd.read_parquet(f, columns=["PULocationID", "fare_amount"])
    print(f"{f:32s} {os.path.getsize(f)/1e6:8.1f} MB  {time.perf_counter()-t0:6.2f} s")

Typical result: Parquet is 5–10× smaller and 10–50× faster to read two columns.

docs.title: 3.4 Apache Arrow: the common language
docs.text:
Before Arrow, moving data from pandas to Spark meant serialising every value. Apache Arrow defines a standard in-memory columnar format. Tools that speak Arrow (pandas, Polars, DuckDB, Spark, R, Julia) can share data with little or no copying.

import pyarrow as pa, pyarrow.compute as pc, polars as pl, duckdb

table = pq.read_table("data/yellow_2024_01.parquet", columns=["PULocationID", "fare_amount"])
print(pc.mean(table["fare_amount"]))

pl_df = pl.from_arrow(table)                                  # zero-copy where possible
print(duckdb.sql("SELECT PULocationID, avg(fare_amount) FROM table GROUP BY 1 LIMIT 5"))

DuckDB can query the local Python variable table directly — that is Arrow at work. In Spark, setting spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled=true speeds up toPandas() and pandas UDFs.

docs.title: 3.5 Partitioning datasets
docs.text:
A partitioned dataset is a directory tree where folder names encode column values (Hive-style):

trips/
├── year=2024/
│   ├── month=01/part-0.parquet
│   ├── month=02/part-0.parquet
│   └── ...
└── year=2025/...

A query filtering year=2024 AND month=02 reads one folder — partition pruning.

import pyarrow.dataset as ds

df["year"] = df.tpep_pickup_datetime.dt.year
df["month"] = df.tpep_pickup_datetime.dt.month
pq.write_to_dataset(pa.Table.from_pandas(df), root_path="data/trips_part",
                    partition_cols=["year", "month"])

dataset = ds.dataset("data/trips_part", format="parquet", partitioning="hive")
feb = dataset.to_table(filter=(ds.field("month") == 2), columns=["fare_amount"])

docs.title: Choosing partition columns
docs.text:
• Partition on columns that appear in most filters and have low-to-moderate cardinality (date, country, district).
  • Never partition on high-cardinality columns (user ID, transaction ID): you create millions of tiny files.
  • Target files of ~100 MB–1 GB. Thousands of 1 KB files is the small files problem: listing and opening files dominates the runtime, and metadata overloads the storage system.

docs.title: 3.6 Where files live: from HDFS to object storage
docs.text:
System Description Local disk Fine for one machine HDFS Hadoop Distributed File System: files split into 128 MB blocks, each replicated 3× across machines; compute moves to the blocks Object storage (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob, MinIO) Today's default: cheap, practically unlimited, accessed over HTTP; compute and storage are separated

Most Python tools read object storage directly, e.g. pd.read_parquet("s3://bucket/path/"), duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM 's3://...'"), spark.read.parquet("s3a://..."). Many public datasets in this course live in AWS S3 buckets with free access (see Data sources).

docs.title: 3.7 Warehouses, lakes and lakehouses
docs.text:
Data warehouse Data lake Lakehouse Storage Proprietary, inside the database Files (Parquet, JSON, images) in object storage Files in object storage plus a transaction log Schema Schema-on-write (strict) Schema-on-read (flexible) Enforced, evolvable Updates / deletes Yes, ACID Painful (rewrite files) Yes, ACID Data types Structured Anything Anything Examples BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift S3 + Parquet Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi

A plain data lake has problems: two jobs writing at once corrupt a table; deleting one person's records (a legal right under data protection law!) means rewriting files; there is no history. Table formats solve these by adding a metadata/transaction log next to the Parquet files, giving:

  • ACID transactions (atomic commits; readers never see half-written data);
  • UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE (upsert);
  • time travel (query the table as of yesterday);
  • schema evolution and enforcement.
# Delta Lake without Spark, via the deltalake (delta-rs) package
# pip install deltalake
from deltalake import write_deltalake, DeltaTable

write_deltalake("data/trips_delta", df[["PULocationID", "fare_amount"]].head(1000))
write_deltalake("data/trips_delta", df[["PULocationID", "fare_amount"]].iloc[1000:2000], mode="append")

dt = DeltaTable("data/trips_delta")
print(dt.version(), len(dt.to_pandas()))
print(len(DeltaTable("data/trips_delta", version=0).to_pandas()))   # time travel: 1000 rows

docs.title: 3.8 NoSQL in one page
docs.text:
Not all big data is tabular files. NoSQL ("not only SQL") databases trade some relational features for scale or flexibility:

Family Data model Strengths Examples Key-value key → blob Extreme speed, caching, sessions Redis, DynamoDB Document JSON-like documents Flexible schema, nested data MongoDB, Couchbase Wide-column Rows with dynamic columns, partitioned by key Huge write throughput, time series Cassandra, HBase, ScyllaDB Graph Nodes and edges Relationship queries Neo4j, JanusGraph Search Inverted index Full-text search, logs Elasticsearch, OpenSearch

The CAP theorem (Chapter 4) explains the consistency trade-offs these systems make.

docs.title: 4. Distributed computing & MapReduce
docs.text:
Learning objectives

  • Describe the architecture of a cluster: driver/master, workers, storage, network.
  • Explain data parallelism, partitioning, and the cost of a shuffle.
  • Express computations in the MapReduce model and implement a MapReduce engine in Python.
  • Explain fault tolerance through replication and recomputation.
  • State the CAP theorem and apply it to real systems.

docs.title: 4.1 Why distributed computing is hard
docs.text:
The "fallacies of distributed computing" (Peter Deutsch and colleagues at Sun) are assumptions that newcomers make and that are false:

  1. The network is reliable.
  2. Latency is zero.
  3. Bandwidth is infinite.
  4. The network is secure.
  5. Topology doesn't change.
  6. There is one administrator.
  7. Transport cost is zero.
  8. The network is homogeneous.

With 1,000 machines each failing on average once every three years, you expect roughly one failure per day. Big data frameworks exist so that you, the analyst, do not have to handle these issues by hand.

docs.title: 4.2 Anatomy of a cluster
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    U[You: notebook / script] --> D[Driver / master<br/>plans the job, schedules tasks]
    D --> W1[Worker 1<br/>executes tasks on partitions]
    D --> W2[Worker 2]
    D --> W3[Worker 3]
    W1 <--> S[(Distributed storage<br/>HDFS / S3)]
    W2 <--> S
    W3 <--> S
    W1 <-. shuffle .-> W2
    W2 <-. shuffle .-> W3
  • Data is split into partitions (chunks), e.g. HDFS blocks or Parquet row groups.
  • A task is one unit of work on one partition. With 1,000 partitions and 100 cores, tasks run in ~10 waves.
  • Data locality: the scheduler prefers to run a task on the machine that already holds its partition.

docs.title: 4.3 Narrow versus wide operations
docs.text:
Narrow (no data movement) Wide (requires a shuffle) map, filter, select columns, add a column groupBy + aggregate, join, distinct, orderBy, repartition Each output partition depends on one input partition Each output partition needs data from many input partitions

A shuffle redistributes records across the network so that all records with the same key land on the same machine. It involves serialising data, writing to local disk, network transfer, and reading back. Shuffles are the main cost of distributed jobs; much of performance tuning (Chapter 7) is about avoiding or shrinking them.

docs.title: 4.4 The MapReduce model
docs.text:
MapReduce expresses a computation as two user functions:

\[ \text{map}: (k_1, v_1) \rightarrow \text{list}(k_2, v_2) \qquad \text{reduce}: (k_2, \text{list}(v_2)) \rightarrow \text{list}(v_3) \]

The framework does everything else: split input, run maps in parallel, shuffle and sort by \(k_2\), run reduces in parallel, handle failures.

flowchart LR
    I1[Split 1] --> M1[map]
    I2[Split 2] --> M2[map]
    I3[Split 3] --> M3[map]
    M1 --> SH{shuffle & sort<br/>by key}
    M2 --> SH
    M3 --> SH
    SH --> R1[reduce: keys A–M]
    SH --> R2[reduce: keys N–Z]
    R1 --> O1[Output 1]
    R2 --> O2[Output 2]

docs.title: Word count, the "hello world" of big data
docs.text:
map("doc1", "umuganda is community work")  → (umuganda,1) (is,1) (community,1) (work,1)
map("doc2", "community work on saturday")   → (community,1) (work,1) (on,1) (saturday,1)
shuffle → community:[1,1]  work:[1,1]  umuganda:[1] ...
reduce("community", [1,1]) → (community, 2)

A combiner is a mini-reduce run on each mapper's output before the shuffle, turning (work,1),(work,1),(work,1) into (work,3) locally. It is valid when the reduce function is associative and commutative (sum, max — but not mean, unless you carry (sum, count) as in Chapter 2).

docs.title: Build your own MapReduce engine
docs.text:
This is the core lab of the chapter. It runs on one machine using processes, but has exactly the structure of Hadoop.

minimr.py
from collections import defaultdict
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
from itertools import chain
import hashlib

def _partition(key, n_reducers):
    """Deterministic hash partitioner (Python's hash() is randomised per process)."""
    return int(hashlib.md5(str(key).encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % n_reducers

def _map_task(args):
    mapper, combiner, chunk, n_reducers = args
    buckets = [defaultdict(list) for _ in range(n_reducers)]
    for record in chunk:
        for k, v in mapper(record):
            buckets[_partition(k, n_reducers)][k].append(v)
    if combiner:                                   # local pre-aggregation
        buckets = [{k: [combiner(k, vs)] for k, vs in b.items()} for b in buckets]
    return buckets

def _reduce_task(args):
    reducer, groups = args
    return [(k, reducer(k, vs)) for k, vs in sorted(groups.items())]

def map_reduce(records, mapper, reducer, combiner=None, n_mappers=4, n_reducers=2):
    records = list(records)
    size = max(1, len(records) // n_mappers + 1)
    chunks = [records[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(records), size)]
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(n_mappers) as ex:
        map_out = list(ex.map(_map_task, [(mapper, combiner, c, n_reducers) for c in chunks]))
        # shuffle: gather bucket r from every mapper
        shuffled = []
        for r in range(n_reducers):
            merged = defaultdict(list)
            for buckets in map_out:
                for k, vs in buckets[r].items():
                    merged[k].extend(vs)
            shuffled.append(merged)
        red_out = list(ex.map(_reduce_task, [(reducer, g) for g in shuffled]))
    return list(chain.from_iterable(red_out))
wordcount.py
import re
from minimr import map_reduce

def mapper(line):
    for w in re.findall(r"[a-zà-ÿ']+", line.lower()):
        yield w, 1

def reducer(word, counts):
    return sum(counts)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    lines = open("corpus.txt", encoding="utf-8")
    result = map_reduce(lines, mapper, reducer, combiner=reducer)
    for w, c in sorted(result, key=lambda x: -x[1])[:20]:
        print(w, c)

docs.title: 4.5 Fault tolerance
docs.text:
Two strategies:

  1. Replication of data. HDFS stores each block on 3 machines. Losing a disk loses nothing.
  2. Re-execution of tasks. Map and reduce functions are deterministic and side-effect free, so a failed task is simply re-run elsewhere. Hadoop writes intermediate results to disk for this reason — making it robust but slow for iterative algorithms.

Spark's insight (Chapter 6): instead of writing every intermediate result to disk, remember the lineage — the recipe of transformations that produced each partition — and recompute lost partitions on demand. Keep data in memory between steps. This makes iterative machine learning 10–100× faster than Hadoop MapReduce.

Stragglers: one slow machine delays the whole stage. Frameworks launch speculative backup copies of slow tasks and take whichever finishes first.

docs.title: 4.6 The CAP theorem
docs.text:
In a distributed data store, when a network partition (P) occurs — some machines cannot talk to others — you must choose between:

  • Consistency (C): every read sees the most recent write;
  • Availability (A): every request receives a (non-error) response.

You cannot have both during a partition. Partitions will happen, so the real choice is C or A when they do.

System behaviour during a partition Choice Examples Refuse writes/reads that might be stale CP HBase, MongoDB (default majority settings), ZooKeeper, banking ledgers Keep answering, reconcile later AP Cassandra, DynamoDB (default), DNS

Example — mobile money. A balance must never be double-spent: choose consistency for the ledger. A "recent transactions" display can tolerate being seconds stale: choose availability.

The PACELC extension adds: Else (no partition), trade Latency against Consistency.

docs.title: 4.7 Hadoop today
docs.text: Hadoop MapReduce is rarely used for new projects, but its ideas — HDFS, partitioning, shuffle, YARN resource management — live on inside Spark, Dask, Flink and cloud services. Understanding MapReduce makes every later tool easier to reason about.

docs.title: 5. Polars, DuckDB & Dask
docs.text:
Learning objectives

  • Explain lazy evaluation and query optimisation and why they matter for big data.
  • Write the same analysis in Polars, DuckDB (SQL) and Dask.
  • Process datasets larger than RAM on a single machine with streaming execution.
  • Choose between these tools and Spark for a given problem.

Modern single-node engines handle tens to hundreds of gigabytes on a laptop. Before you rent a cluster, try these.

docs.title: 5.1 Eager versus lazy evaluation
docs.text:
Eager (pandas): every line runs immediately and materialises a full intermediate result.

Lazy (Polars LazyFrame, Dask, Spark, DuckDB SQL): each line adds a step to a query plan; nothing runs until you ask for a result. The engine can then optimise the whole plan:

  • Projection pushdown — read only needed columns.
  • Predicate pushdown — apply filters while reading (using Parquet statistics).
  • Operator fusion — combine steps into one pass over the data.
  • Streaming — process the data in batches, never holding it all in memory.
flowchart LR
    A[scan_parquet<br/>all 19 columns] --> B[with_columns tip_pct] --> C[filter fare > 0] --> D[group_by zone] --> E[select 2 cols]
    A2[scan only 3 columns<br/>filter during scan] --> D2[compute + group_by in streaming batches]
    E -. optimiser rewrites .-> A2

docs.title: 5.2 Polars
docs.text: Polars is a DataFrame library written in Rust, built on Arrow, multi-threaded by default, with an expressive expression API.

docs.title: Eager basics
docs.text:
import polars as pl

df = pl.read_parquet("data/yellow_2024_01.parquet")
print(df.schema)

out = (
    df.filter(pl.col("fare_amount") > 0)
      .with_columns((100 * pl.col("tip_amount") / pl.col("fare_amount")).alias("tip_pct"))
      .group_by("PULocationID")
      .agg(pl.len().alias("trips"),
           pl.col("tip_pct").mean().alias("mean_tip_pct"),
           pl.col("trip_distance").median().alias("median_km"))
      .sort("trips", descending=True)
)
print(out.head())

docs.title: Expressions are the key idea
docs.text:
pl.col("fare_amount") > 0 is not computed immediately; it is an expression that Polars can optimise and run in parallel across columns.

df.select(
    pl.col("tpep_pickup_datetime").dt.hour().alias("hour"),
    pl.col("^.*_amount$").sum(),                       # regex: all amount columns
    pl.when(pl.col("trip_distance") > 10).then(pl.lit("long"))
      .otherwise(pl.lit("short")).alias("trip_type"),
)

docs.title: Lazy and streaming: larger than memory
docs.text:
lazy = (
    pl.scan_parquet("data/yellow_2024_*.parquet")      # glob over many files, nothing read yet
      .filter(pl.col("fare_amount") > 0)
      .group_by(pl.col("tpep_pickup_datetime").dt.month().alias("month"))
      .agg(pl.len(), pl.col("total_amount").sum())
      .sort("month")
)
print(lazy.explain())                 # inspect the optimised plan
result = lazy.collect(engine="streaming")   # batch-wise execution, low memory

Look for PROJECT 3/19 COLUMNS and SELECTION inside the scan in the plan: proof of pushdown.

docs.title: Window functions and joins
docs.text:
zones = pl.read_csv("https://d37ci6vzurychx.cloudfront.net/misc/taxi_zone_lookup.csv")

ranked = (
    df.lazy()
      .join(zones.lazy(), left_on="PULocationID", right_on="LocationID")
      .group_by(["Borough", "Zone"]).agg(pl.len().alias("trips"))
      .with_columns(pl.col("trips").rank(descending=True).over("Borough").alias("rank_in_borough"))
      .filter(pl.col("rank_in_borough") <= 3)
      .collect()
)

docs.title: 5.3 DuckDB
docs.text:
DuckDB is an in-process analytical SQL database — "SQLite for analytics". There is no server; it runs inside Python, queries Parquet/CSV/JSON files directly (including over HTTP and S3), spills to disk when memory runs out, and uses all cores.

import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()            # in-memory; use duckdb.connect("lab.duckdb") to persist

con.sql("""
    SELECT PULocationID,
           count(*)                          AS trips,
           avg(tip_amount / fare_amount)*100 AS mean_tip_pct,
           quantile_cont(trip_distance, 0.5) AS median_km
    FROM 'data/yellow_2024_*.parquet'
    WHERE fare_amount > 0
    GROUP BY 1
    ORDER BY trips DESC
    LIMIT 10
""").show()

docs.title: Query remote files without downloading
docs.text:
con.sql("INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;")
con.sql("""
    SELECT count(*), avg(trip_distance)
    FROM 'https://d37ci6vzurychx.cloudfront.net/trip-data/yellow_tripdata_2024-03.parquet'
""").show()

Because of Parquet footers and HTTP range requests, DuckDB fetches only the bytes it needs.

docs.title: Mix SQL and DataFrames
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
zones = pd.read_csv("https://d37ci6vzurychx.cloudfront.net/misc/taxi_zone_lookup.csv")

top = con.sql("""
    SELECT z.Borough, count(*) AS trips
    FROM 'data/yellow_2024_01.parquet' t
    JOIN zones z ON t.PULocationID = z.LocationID
    GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC
""").pl()          # .df() for pandas, .arrow() for Arrow, .pl() for Polars

docs.title: Useful features
docs.text:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ...;                          -- plan with timings
COPY (SELECT * FROM 'raw/*.csv') TO 'clean' (FORMAT parquet, PARTITION_BY (year, month));
SUMMARIZE SELECT * FROM 'data/yellow_2024_01.parquet';   -- instant data profile
SET memory_limit = '4GB'; SET threads = 4;

docs.title: 5.4 Dask
docs.text:
Dask parallelises the familiar pandas and NumPy APIs by splitting data into many smaller pandas DataFrames (partitions) and building a task graph. It scales from a laptop to a cluster with the same code.

import dask.dataframe as dd
from dask.distributed import Client

client = Client()            # local cluster: one worker per core; dashboard link printed
print(client.dashboard_link)

ddf = dd.read_parquet("data/yellow_2024_*.parquet",
                      columns=["PULocationID", "fare_amount", "tip_amount", "trip_distance"])
print(ddf.npartitions)

result = (ddf[ddf.fare_amount > 0]
          .assign(tip_pct=lambda d: 100 * d.tip_amount / d.fare_amount)
          .groupby("PULocationID")
          .agg({"tip_pct": "mean", "trip_distance": ["mean", "max"]}))

result.visualize("graph.png")   # optional: draw the task graph (needs graphviz)
pdf = result.compute()          # execute → pandas DataFrame

docs.title: Dask beyond DataFrames
docs.text:
import dask.array as da
x = da.random.random((100_000, 10_000), chunks=(10_000, 10_000))   # 8 GB, never all in RAM
print((x - x.mean(axis=0)).std(axis=0)[:5].compute())

import dask
@dask.delayed
def process(path): ...
results = dask.compute(*[process(p) for p in paths])   # parallelise arbitrary Python

Dask arrays power xarray for climate and satellite data (Chapter 10), and Dask-ML for scalable scikit-learn (Chapter 8). Open the dashboard while jobs run: the task stream, progress bars and memory panels are excellent teaching tools.

docs.title: 5.5 Choosing a tool
docs.text:
Situation Recommended Data fits comfortably in RAM, team knows pandas pandas (with Arrow dtypes) 1–200 GB on one machine, DataFrame style Polars (lazy + streaming) 1–200 GB on one machine, SQL style, ad-hoc exploration of files DuckDB Need the pandas/NumPy/scikit-learn API on multiple machines, or arbitrary Python task parallelism, or n-dimensional arrays Dask Multi-terabyte data, shared clusters, streaming, mature ecosystem, JVM integration Spark (Chapters 6–9)

These tools interoperate through Arrow, so you can mix them in one notebook.

docs.title: Lab 5 — Three engines, one question

Using 3–12 months of NYC yellow taxi data (choose a size that is larger than comfortable for pandas on your machine):

Question: for each hour of the day and day of the week, what is the median trip speed (km/h) in Manhattan? (Distance is in miles: multiply by 1.609.)

  3. Print the Polars plan and DuckDB EXPLAIN output; identify the pushdowns.
  4. Plot a heatmap (hour × weekday) of median speed.
  5. Write a half-page recommendation: which engine would you choose for this team, and why?

docs.title: 6. Apache Spark fundamentals
docs.text:
Learning objectives

  • Describe Spark's architecture: driver, executors, cluster manager, jobs, stages, tasks.
  • Explain RDDs, lineage and lazy evaluation.
  • Distinguish transformations from actions, and narrow from wide transformations.
  • Read, transform, aggregate and write data with the PySpark DataFrame API.
  • Use the Spark UI to understand what a job did.

docs.title: 6.1 What is Spark?
docs.text: Apache Spark is a unified engine for large-scale data processing. One API covers batch SQL and DataFrames, machine learning (MLlib), streaming (Structured Streaming) and graph processing. Programs are written in Python (PySpark), Scala, Java, R or SQL. The current release line is Spark 4.x, which requires Java 17+ and Python 3.9+, enables ANSI SQL mode by default, and makes Spark Connect (a thin client–server protocol) a first-class way to connect.

docs.title: 6.2 Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Driver["Driver (your PySpark program)"]
      SS[SparkSession] --> DAG[DAG scheduler:<br/>job → stages]
      DAG --> TS[Task scheduler]
    end
    TS --> CM[Cluster manager<br/>local / Standalone / YARN / Kubernetes]
    CM --> E1[Executor 1<br/>cores + memory + cache]
    CM --> E2[Executor 2]
    CM --> E3[Executor 3]
    E1 -. shuffle .- E2
    E2 -. shuffle .- E3
Term Meaning Driver Process running your main program; builds the plan and schedules work Executor JVM process on a worker that runs tasks and caches data Cluster manager Allocates executors: local[*] (all cores of your laptop), Standalone, YARN, Kubernetes Job Triggered by each action (e.g. count(), write) Stage A set of tasks that can run without a shuffle; jobs are split at shuffle boundaries Task Work on one partition, on one core

In local[*] mode, the driver and executors run inside one process on your laptop — perfect for learning; the same code runs unchanged on a 500-node cluster.

docs.title: 6.3 Starting Spark
docs.text:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F, types as T

spark = (SparkSession.builder
         .appName("aims-bda-lab6")
         .master("local[*]")
         .config("spark.driver.memory", "4g")
         .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "16")   # default 200 is too many for a laptop
         .getOrCreate())

print(spark.version)
print(spark.sparkContext.uiWebUrl)   # open the Spark UI, usually http://localhost:4040

Databricks and Spark Connect

On Databricks, spark already exists. With Spark Connect you write SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://host:15002").getOrCreate(); the DataFrame API is the same, but the low-level RDD API is not available.

docs.title: 6.4 RDDs: the foundation
docs.text:
A Resilient Distributed Dataset is an immutable, partitioned collection of records, plus its lineage — the chain of transformations used to build it. If a partition is lost, Spark recomputes it from lineage.

sc = spark.sparkContext
rdd = sc.parallelize(range(1, 1_000_001), numSlices=8)
print(rdd.getNumPartitions())

squares = rdd.map(lambda x: x * x)          # transformation (lazy)
evens = squares.filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0)
print(evens.count())                         # action → runs the job
print(evens.toDebugString().decode())        # lineage

Word count, now in Spark — compare it with your MapReduce engine from Chapter 4:

counts = (sc.textFile("data/corpus.txt")
            .flatMap(lambda line: line.lower().split())
            .map(lambda w: (w, 1))
            .reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b)       # combiner + shuffle + reduce
            .sortBy(lambda kv: -kv[1]))
print(counts.take(10))

reduceByKey combines locally before shuffling; groupByKey ships every value across the network. Prefer reduceByKey/aggregateByKey.

Why we mostly use DataFrames instead: RDD lambdas are opaque Python functions that Spark cannot optimise, and each record crosses the Python–JVM boundary. DataFrame operations are declarative, so Spark's Catalyst optimiser rewrites them and the Tungsten engine runs them as compiled JVM code with no Python overhead.

docs.title: 6.5 Transformations and actions
docs.text:
Transformations (lazy, return a new DataFrame) Actions (trigger execution) select, filter/where, withColumn, drop count, show, collect, take, first groupBy().agg(), join, union, distinct, orderBy write..., toPandas, foreach

Beware of collect() and toPandas()

They bring the entire result to the driver's memory. On a billion-row DataFrame they crash the driver. Aggregate or limit() first.

docs.title: Reading data
docs.text:
trips = spark.read.parquet("data/yellow_2024_*.parquet")
trips.printSchema()
print(trips.count(), len(trips.columns))

zones = (spark.read
         .option("header", True)
         .option("inferSchema", True)
         .csv("data/taxi_zone_lookup.csv"))

For CSV and JSON in production, declare the schema — inference requires an extra pass over the data and may guess wrong:

schema = T.StructType([
    T.StructField("LocationID", T.IntegerType()),
    T.StructField("Borough", T.StringType()),
    T.StructField("Zone", T.StringType()),
    T.StructField("service_zone", T.StringType()),
])
zones = spark.read.csv("data/taxi_zone_lookup.csv", header=True, schema=schema)

docs.title: Selecting, filtering, deriving columns
docs.text:
clean = (trips
    .filter((F.col("fare_amount") > 0) & (F.col("trip_distance").between(0.1, 100)))
    .withColumn("duration_min",
                (F.unix_timestamp("tpep_dropoff_datetime") -
                 F.unix_timestamp("tpep_pickup_datetime")) / 60)
    .filter(F.col("duration_min").between(1, 180))
    .withColumn("speed_kmh", F.col("trip_distance") * 1.609 / (F.col("duration_min") / 60))
    .withColumn("pickup_hour", F.hour("tpep_pickup_datetime"))
    .withColumn("pickup_dow", F.dayofweek("tpep_pickup_datetime"))
    .withColumn("is_airport", F.col("RatecodeID").isin(2, 3))
    .select("tpep_pickup_datetime", "PULocationID", "DOLocationID", "pickup_hour", "pickup_dow",
            "trip_distance", "duration_min", "speed_kmh", "fare_amount",
            "tip_amount", "payment_type", "is_airport"))
clean.show(5)

docs.title: Aggregation
docs.text:
by_hour = (clean.groupBy("pickup_hour")
           .agg(F.count("*").alias("trips"),
                F.round(F.avg("speed_kmh"), 1).alias("avg_speed"),
                F.percentile_approx("fare_amount", 0.5).alias("median_fare"),
                F.sum("tip_amount").alias("total_tips"))
           .orderBy("pickup_hour"))
by_hour.show(24)

docs.title: Joins
docs.text:
enriched = clean.join(zones.withColumnRenamed("LocationID", "PULocationID"),
                      on="PULocationID", how="left")
(enriched.groupBy("Borough").count().orderBy(F.desc("count")).show())

docs.title: Handling missing values and conditional logic
docs.text:
trips.select([F.sum(F.col(c).isNull().cast("int")).alias(c) for c in trips.columns]).show(vertical=True)

trips = (trips
    .fillna({"passenger_count": 1})
    .withColumn("payment",
                F.when(F.col("payment_type") == 1, "card")
                 .when(F.col("payment_type") == 2, "cash")
                 .otherwise("other")))

docs.title: Writing results
docs.text:
(by_hour.coalesce(1).write.mode("overwrite").option("header", True).csv("out/by_hour_csv"))
(enriched.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("Borough").parquet("out/trips_by_borough"))

Spark writes a directory of part files (one per partition), plus a _SUCCESS marker — not a single file. coalesce(1) forces one file; use it only for small outputs.

docs.title: Spark SQL
docs.text:
Every DataFrame can be queried with SQL; both compile to the same plan.

clean.createOrReplaceTempView("trips")
spark.sql("""
    SELECT pickup_dow, pickup_hour, percentile_approx(speed_kmh, 0.5) AS median_speed
    FROM trips
    GROUP BY pickup_dow, pickup_hour
    ORDER BY pickup_dow, pickup_hour
""").show()

docs.title: 6.7 Lazy evaluation and the DAG in practice
docs.text:
q = clean.groupBy("PULocationID").agg(F.avg("fare_amount").alias("avg_fare"))
q.explain(mode="formatted")

In the physical plan, look for:

  • FileScan parquet ... ReadSchema: — only the needed columns (projection pushdown);
  • PushedFilters: — filters applied at the source;
  • HashAggregate (partial) → Exchange hashpartitioning → HashAggregate (final) — the combiner, the shuffle, and the reduce, exactly as in Chapter 4.

Now run q.show() and open the Spark UI (port 4040): Jobs → one job; Stages → two stages separated by the Exchange; each stage's task count equals its partition count; the SQL / DataFrame tab shows the same plan with row counts.

docs.title: 6.8 Partitions
docs.text:
print(trips.rdd.getNumPartitions())          # set by file sizes (~128 MB per input split)
fewer = trips.coalesce(4)                    # merge partitions, no full shuffle
more = trips.repartition(64, "PULocationID") # full shuffle, hash by key

Rules of thumb: 2–4 tasks per core; partitions of roughly 100–200 MB; set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to match data size (or rely on Adaptive Query Execution, Chapter 7).

docs.title: 6.9 Caching
docs.text:
If you reuse a DataFrame in several actions, cache it, or Spark recomputes it from the source each time.

clean.cache()          # or .persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK)
clean.count()          # first action materialises the cache
# ... many queries on clean ...
clean.unpersist()

Check the Storage tab of the Spark UI to see what is cached and how much memory it uses.

docs.title: 6.10 Python UDFs — and how to avoid them
docs.text:
A plain Python UDF sends each row from the JVM to a Python worker and back: slow.

# Slow: row-at-a-time Python UDF
@F.udf(T.StringType())
def fare_band(f):
    return "low" if f < 10 else "mid" if f < 30 else "high"

# Fast: built-in expressions (runs in the JVM)
band = F.when(F.col("fare_amount") < 10, "low").when(F.col("fare_amount") < 30, "mid").otherwise("high")

# When you really need Python: vectorised pandas UDF (Arrow batches)
import pandas as pd
@F.pandas_udf(T.DoubleType())
def log1p_fare(s: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    import numpy as np
    return np.log1p(s)

clean.select(band.alias("band"), log1p_fare("fare_amount").alias("lf")).show(3)

Order of preference: built-in functions (pyspark.sql.functions) → SQL expressions → pandas UDFs → Python UDFs.

docs.title: Lab 6 — Your first Spark analysis
docs.text:
Using 3+ months of NYC taxi data (or the Databricks sample samples.nyctaxi.trips on Databricks):

docs.title: 7. Spark SQL & performance tuning
docs.text:
Learning objectives

  • Use window functions, complex types and higher-order functions for advanced analytics.
  • Explain how the Catalyst optimiser and Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) transform queries.
  • Choose join strategies (broadcast hash, sort-merge, shuffle hash) and force them when needed.

  • Work with lakehouse tables (Delta Lake) from Spark.

docs.title: 7.1 Window functions
docs.text:
A window function computes a value for each row using a group of related rows, without collapsing them (unlike groupBy).

from pyspark.sql import Window, functions as F

daily = (clean.withColumn("date", F.to_date("tpep_pickup_datetime"))   # clean from Chapter 6
         .groupBy("PULocationID", "date").agg(F.count("*").alias("trips")))

w_zone = Window.partitionBy("PULocationID").orderBy("date")
w_7d   = w_zone.rowsBetween(-6, 0)

features = (daily
    .withColumn("trips_lag1", F.lag("trips", 1).over(w_zone))
    .withColumn("trips_7d_avg", F.avg("trips").over(w_7d))
    .withColumn("growth", (F.col("trips") - F.col("trips_lag1")) / F.col("trips_lag1"))
    .withColumn("rank_today", F.dense_rank().over(
        Window.partitionBy("date").orderBy(F.desc("trips")))))
features.filter("rank_today <= 3").orderBy("date", "rank_today").show()

Common window functions: row_number, rank, dense_rank, lag, lead, ntile, cume_dist, running sum/avg with frames. They are essential for time-series features (Chapter 8) and sessionisation.

Windows without partitionBy

Window.orderBy("date") with no partition moves all data to one task. Spark warns about this. Always partition when possible.

docs.title: 7.2 Complex and nested data
docs.text:
Real big data (JSON logs, API responses, GDELT, GitHub events) is nested. Spark handles struct, array and map types natively.

events = spark.read.json("data/gharchive/2024-01-01-*.json.gz")   # GitHub Archive
events.printSchema()

pushes = (events.filter(F.col("type") == "PushEvent")
          .select("actor.login", "repo.name",
                  F.explode("payload.commits").alias("commit"))
          .select("login", "name", F.col("commit.message").alias("msg")))

# Higher-order functions on arrays — no explode/regroup needed
df = spark.createDataFrame([(1, [3, 8, 1]), (2, [10, 2])], ["id", "xs"])
df.select("id",
          F.transform("xs", lambda x: x * 2).alias("doubled"),
          F.filter("xs", lambda x: x > 2).alias("big"),
          F.aggregate("xs", F.lit(0), lambda acc, x: acc + x).alias("total")).show()

docs.title: 7.3 How Spark optimises your query
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Q[DataFrame / SQL] --> UL[Unresolved<br/>logical plan]
    UL -->|Analysis: resolve names, types| LP[Logical plan]
    LP -->|Catalyst rules: pushdown,<br/>constant folding, pruning| OLP[Optimised<br/>logical plan]
    OLP -->|Cost-based planning| PP[Physical plans]
    PP --> SP[Selected physical plan]
    SP -->|Whole-stage codegen| RDD[Compiled JVM code]
    SP -. AQE re-plans at runtime .-> SP

Adaptive Query Execution (AQE), on by default since Spark 3.2, re-optimises during execution using real statistics from completed stages:

  • coalesces small shuffle partitions (so spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=200 is less harmful);
  • switches sort-merge joins to broadcast joins when a side turns out small;
  • splits skewed partitions in joins.
spark.conf.get("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled")                  # 'true'
q.explain(mode="formatted")   # AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false before running, true after

docs.title: 7.4 Join strategies
docs.text:
Strategy When Cost Broadcast hash join One side is small (default threshold 10 MB; raise with care) Small side copied to every executor; no shuffle of the big side Sort-merge join Both sides large Both sides shuffled and sorted by key Shuffle hash join One side medium, fits in memory per partition Both shuffled, hash table built 
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

joined = trips.join(broadcast(zones), trips.PULocationID == zones.LocationID)
joined.explain()   # look for BroadcastHashJoin

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", 50 * 1024 * 1024)  # 50 MB

Joining 3 billion mobile money records with a 300-row district table should always be a broadcast join.

docs.title: 7.5 Data skew
docs.text:
Skew means a few keys have far more records than others, so a few tasks run much longer than the rest. Symptoms in the Spark UI → Stages → task summary: max duration ≫ median, one task with huge "Shuffle Read Size", and the stage stuck at "199/200".

Examples: one airport zone with 20% of trips; a "null" or "unknown" key; one celebrity account in a social graph.

Fixes, in order of preference:

  1. Let AQE handle it (spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true, default on).
  2. Filter or handle bad keys separately (e.g., nulls).
  3. Broadcast the smaller side if possible.
  4. Salting: add a random suffix to the hot key to spread it across tasks.
N = 16  # salt buckets
big_salted = big.withColumn("salt", (F.rand() * N).cast("int"))
small_salted = small.crossJoin(spark.range(N).withColumnRenamed("id", "salt"))
result = big_salted.join(small_salted, ["key", "salt"]).drop("salt")

For skewed aggregations, use two-stage aggregation: aggregate by (key, salt) first, then by key.

docs.title: 7.6 Memory, spills and the small files problem
docs.text:
Executor memory is divided into execution memory (shuffles, joins, sorts) and storage memory (cache). When execution memory is insufficient, Spark spills to disk — visible as "Spill (Memory)" and "Spill (Disk)" in the stage page. Fixes: more partitions (smaller tasks), more executor memory, avoid exploding rows unnecessarily.

Small files: reading 100,000 tiny files is slow because of per-file overhead. When writing:

(df.repartition("year", "month")              # one task per partition value → fewer files
   .write.partitionBy("year", "month").mode("overwrite").parquet("out/trips"))

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.files.maxRecordsPerFile", 5_000_000)

docs.title: 7.7 A tuning checklist
docs.text:
1. Read only what you need: Parquet, column selection, early filters, partition pruning.
  2. Avoid Python UDFs; use built-in functions or pandas UDFs.
  3. Broadcast small dimension tables.
  4. Check partition counts: 2–4 per core, ~100–200 MB each; trust AQE but verify.
  5. Cache only DataFrames reused multiple times; unpersist afterwards.
  6. Never collect() large data; aggregate first.
  7. Look at the Spark UI: the longest stage, its skew, its spill, its shuffle size.
  8. Change one thing at a time and measure.

docs.title: 8. Machine learning at scale
docs.text:
Learning objectives

  • Explain why and when machine learning needs distributed computation.
  • Derive distributed gradient descent and understand what is parallelised.
  • Build end-to-end Spark MLlib pipelines: feature engineering, training, evaluation, tuning, persistence.
  • Avoid leakage and evaluate correctly on large, time-ordered data.
  • Scale scikit-learn workflows with Dask and apply trained models to big data in batch.

docs.title: 8.1 Do you need distributed ML?
docs.text:
Often, no. A strong workflow is:

  1. Use Spark/DuckDB/Polars to clean and aggregate terabytes into features.
  2. Sample or aggregate to something that fits in memory (often millions of rows are plenty).
  3. Train with scikit-learn, XGBoost or LightGBM on one machine.
  4. Score the full dataset in parallel (pandas UDF or Dask).

Distributed training is warranted when the training set itself is too large for one machine and more data measurably improves the model (learning curves!), or when you must train many models (one per district, per product) in parallel.

# Learning curve: does more data help?
for frac in [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 0.5]:
    sample = train.sample(fraction=frac, seed=42).toPandas()
    ...  # fit, evaluate on fixed validation set, plot score vs n

docs.title: 8.2 The mathematics of data-parallel learning
docs.text:
Most models minimise an average loss over \(n\) examples:

\[ L( heta) = rac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \ell( heta; x_i, y_i), \qquad abla L( heta) = rac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} abla \ell( heta; x_i, y_i). \]

The gradient is a sum over examples — a mergeable statistic (Chapter 2)! Partition the data over \(K\) workers \(P_1,\dots,P_K\):

\[ abla L( heta) = rac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{K} \underbrace{\sum_{i\in P_k} abla \ell( heta; x_i, y_i)}_{g_k ext{ computed on worker } k}. \]

Each iteration: broadcast \( heta\) → each worker computes \(g_k\) on its partition (map) → sum the \(g_k\) (reduce) → update \( heta \leftarrow heta - \eta abla L\) on the driver. This is MapReduce in a loop, and it is why Spark's in-memory caching (versus Hadoop's disk) matters so much.

docs.title: Distributed logistic regression from scratch
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

def sigmoid(z): return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

# rdd of (x: np.ndarray, y: float)
data = (train_df.select("features", "label").rdd
        .map(lambda r: (r.features.toArray(), float(r.label)))
        .cache())
n = data.count(); d = len(data.first()[0])
theta = np.zeros(d); lr = 0.5

for it in range(50):
    b = spark.sparkContext.broadcast(theta)
    grad = data.map(lambda xy: (sigmoid(xy[0] @ b.value) - xy[1]) * xy[0]) \
               .reduce(lambda a, c: a + c) / n
    theta -= lr * grad
    b.unpersist()

Spark MLlib does the same, with better optimisers (L-BFGS, OWL-QN) and treeAggregate to avoid a bottleneck at the driver.

docs.title: Tree models at scale
docs.text: Decision trees are trained by finding the best split per feature. MLlib bins each continuous feature into at most maxBins buckets, then each worker computes histograms of label statistics per bin on its partition; histograms are summed (mergeable!) and the driver picks the best split. Random forests and gradient-boosted trees repeat this per tree/level.

docs.text: Concept Description Examples Transformer transform(df) → df VectorAssembler, a fitted model Estimator fit(df) → Transformer StringIndexer, LogisticRegression Pipeline Chain of stages; itself an Estimator indexers → assembler → scaler → model Evaluator Computes a metric BinaryClassificationEvaluator, RegressionEvaluator Feature vector All features in one vector column output of VectorAssembler

docs.title: 8.4 An end-to-end pipeline
docs.text:
Task: predict whether a card-paid taxi trip receives a tip of at least 20% of the fare (binary classification).

from pyspark.ml import Pipeline
from pyspark.ml.feature import StringIndexer, OneHotEncoder, VectorAssembler, StandardScaler
from pyspark.ml.classification import LogisticRegression, RandomForestClassifier, GBTClassifier
from pyspark.ml.evaluation import BinaryClassificationEvaluator

data = (clean.filter(F.col("payment_type") == 1)
        .withColumn("label", (F.col("tip_amount") >= 0.2 * F.col("fare_amount")).cast("double"))
        .withColumn("PU", F.col("PULocationID").cast("string"))
        .withColumn("DO", F.col("DOLocationID").cast("string"))
        .withColumn("is_weekend", F.col("pickup_dow").isin(1, 7).cast("double"))
        .withColumn("is_airport", F.col("is_airport").cast("double")))

# Time-based split: train on the past, test on the future (no leakage)
train = data.filter(F.month("tpep_pickup_datetime") <= 2)
test  = data.filter(F.month("tpep_pickup_datetime") == 3)
print(train.groupBy("label").count().collect())   # check class balance

cat_cols = ["PU", "DO"]
num_cols = ["trip_distance", "duration_min", "speed_kmh", "pickup_hour",
            "is_weekend", "is_airport", "fare_amount"]

indexers = [StringIndexer(inputCol=c, outputCol=c + "_idx", handleInvalid="keep") for c in cat_cols]
encoder = OneHotEncoder(inputCols=[c + "_idx" for c in cat_cols],
                        outputCols=[c + "_oh" for c in cat_cols])
assembler = VectorAssembler(inputCols=num_cols + [c + "_oh" for c in cat_cols],
                            outputCol="raw_features", handleInvalid="skip")
scaler = StandardScaler(inputCol="raw_features", outputCol="features", withMean=False)
lr = LogisticRegression(featuresCol="features", labelCol="label", maxIter=50, regParam=0.01)

pipeline = Pipeline(stages=indexers + [encoder, assembler, scaler, lr])
model = pipeline.fit(train)

pred = model.transform(test)
auc = BinaryClassificationEvaluator(labelCol="label", metricName="areaUnderROC").evaluate(pred)
pr  = BinaryClassificationEvaluator(labelCol="label", metricName="areaUnderPR").evaluate(pred)
print(f"AUC-ROC {auc:.3f}  AUC-PR {pr:.3f}")

Leakage alert

fare_amount is known at the end of the trip, as is tip_amount. Using total_amount as a feature would leak the tip. Always ask: would I know this value at prediction time?

docs.title: Hyperparameter tuning
docs.text:
from pyspark.ml.tuning import ParamGridBuilder, TrainValidationSplit, CrossValidator

rf = RandomForestClassifier(featuresCol="features", labelCol="label", seed=42)
pipe_rf = Pipeline(stages=indexers + [encoder, assembler, scaler, rf])

grid = (ParamGridBuilder()
        .addGrid(rf.numTrees, [50, 100])
        .addGrid(rf.maxDepth, [6, 10])
        .build())

tvs = TrainValidationSplit(estimator=pipe_rf, estimatorParamMaps=grid,
                           evaluator=BinaryClassificationEvaluator(labelCol="label"),
                           trainRatio=0.8, parallelism=4, seed=42)   # parallelism: models trained concurrently
tvs_model = tvs.fit(train.sample(0.2, seed=1))   # tune on a sample, then refit on all
print(tvs_model.validationMetrics)
best = tvs_model.bestModel

CrossValidator (k-fold) costs \(k\times\) more; on big data, a single validation split is often sufficient and far cheaper.

docs.title: Recommendation with ALS (MovieLens)
docs.text:
Collaborative filtering factorises the sparse user–item rating matrix \(R \approx U V^\top\). ALS alternates: fix \(V\), solve a least-squares problem for each user's row of \(U\) (independently → parallel); then fix \(U\) and solve for \(V\).

from pyspark.ml.recommendation import ALS
from pyspark.ml.evaluation import RegressionEvaluator

ratings = spark.read.csv("data/ml-32m/ratings.csv", header=True, inferSchema=True)
tr, te = ratings.randomSplit([0.8, 0.2], seed=42)
als = ALS(userCol="userId", itemCol="movieId", ratingCol="rating",
          rank=32, regParam=0.05, maxIter=10, coldStartStrategy="drop")
m = als.fit(tr)
print(RegressionEvaluator(labelCol="rating", metricName="rmse").evaluate(m.transform(te)))
m.recommendForAllUsers(10).show(3, truncate=False)

import joblib, pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier

bclf = spark.sparkContext.broadcast(clf)

@F.pandas_udf("double")
def score(trip_distance: pd.Series, duration_min: pd.Series,
          pickup_hour: pd.Series, fare_amount: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    X = pd.concat([trip_distance, duration_min, pickup_hour, fare_amount], axis=1)
    X.columns = feats
    return pd.Series(bclf.value.predict_proba(X)[:, 1])

scored = test.withColumn("p_tip", score(*feats))

docs.title: 8.7 Evaluating on big data: pitfalls
docs.text:
• Time leakage. Random splits on time series leak the future. Split by time.
  • Group leakage. The same customer in train and test inflates scores. Split by customer.
  • Class imbalance. Fraud may be 0.1% of transactions: report AUC-PR, precision@k, recall at fixed false-positive rate, not accuracy. Use weightCol in MLlib for class weights.
  • Statistical vs practical significance. With 100 million test rows, tiny differences are "significant". Ask whether they matter.
  • Distribution shift. A model trained on Kigali data may fail in rural districts. Evaluate on subgroups (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 9. Streaming analytics
docs.text:
Learning objectives

  • Explain event time versus processing time, windows and watermarks.
