docs.title: 9.1 Why streaming?
docs.text:
Some data loses value quickly. Fraud on a mobile money transfer must be stopped before the money moves; a sensor reporting that a water tank is empty matters now, not tomorrow. Streaming systems process unbounded data continuously, producing results with low latency.

Batch Streaming Input Bounded (a file, a table) Unbounded (events keep arriving) Latency Minutes–hours Milliseconds–seconds Typical question "Total sales last month" "Alert if > 5 failed PINs in 2 minutes" Tools Spark, Dask, DuckDB Kafka, Spark Structured Streaming, Apache Flink

docs.title: Event time vs processing time
docs.text:
• Event time: when the event happened (the timestamp inside the record).
  • Processing time: when the system sees it.

On African mobile networks, a phone may buffer transactions offline and upload them an hour later. Analyses must use event time, and must tolerate late and out-of-order data.

docs.title: Watermarks
docs.text:
A watermark says: "I assume no event older than max event time seen − delay will arrive." It lets the engine finalise windows and discard old state, bounding memory. Events later than the watermark are dropped.

\[ \text{watermark} = \max(\text{event time seen}) - \text{allowed lateness} \]

docs.title: Delivery guarantees
docs.text:
• At most once: may lose events.
  • At least once: may duplicate events.
  • Exactly once: each event affects results once. Spark achieves end-to-end exactly-once with replayable sources (Kafka), checkpointing and idempotent/transactional sinks.

docs.title: 9.3 Message brokers: Apache Kafka
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    P1[Producers:<br/>apps, sensors, USSD gateway] --> T[(Kafka topic<br/>partition 0 | partition 1 | partition 2)]
    T --> C1[Consumer group A:<br/>fraud detection]
    T --> C2[Consumer group B:<br/>archive to data lake]

Kafka is a distributed, durable, append-only log. Producers append messages to topics, split into partitions for parallelism; each message has an offset. Consumers read at their own pace and can replay from any offset. This decouples producers from consumers and makes streams replayable — the basis of fault tolerance.

To run Kafka locally for the lab, the labs/docker-compose.yml includes an optional single-node Kafka service (KRaft mode). Python clients: confluent-kafka or kafka-python.

# Producer (pip install confluent-kafka)
from confluent_kafka import Producer
import json, time, random
p = Producer({"bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092"})
for i in range(1000):
    evt = {"txn_id": i, "district": random.choice(["Gasabo", "Huye", "Musanze", "Rubavu"]),
           "amount": round(random.lognormvariate(8, 1)), "ts": time.time()}

docs.title: 9.4 Spark Structured Streaming
docs.text:
Structured Streaming treats a stream as an unbounded table to which rows are continuously appended. You write the same DataFrame code as for batch; Spark runs it incrementally, by default in micro-batches.

flowchart LR
    S[Source: Kafka, files,<br/>socket, rate] --> Q[Streaming DataFrame<br/>same API as batch] --> K[Sink: console, files,<br/>Kafka, Delta, foreachBatch]
    Q --- ST[(State + checkpoint)]

docs.title: First stream: the built-in rate source
docs.text:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[*]").appName("stream").getOrCreate()

stream = (spark.readStream.format("rate").option("rowsPerSecond", 50).load())   # (timestamp, value)

counts = (stream
    .withColumn("district", F.element_at(F.array(*[F.lit(d) for d in
                ["Gasabo", "Huye", "Musanze", "Rubavu"]]), (F.col("value") % 4 + 1).cast("int")))
    .withWatermark("timestamp", "30 seconds")
    .groupBy(F.window("timestamp", "10 seconds"), "district")
    .count())

query = (counts.writeStream
         .outputMode("update")          # append | update | complete
         .format("console")
         .option("truncate", False)
         .trigger(processingTime="5 seconds")
         .start())
query.awaitTermination(60); query.stop()

docs.title: 9.5 Real live data: Wikimedia EventStreams
docs.text:
Wikimedia publishes every edit to every Wikipedia in real time as Server-Sent Events at https://stream.wikimedia.org/v2/stream/recentchange — a free, genuine high-velocity stream (dozens of events per second).

A simple bridge writes events to small JSON files that Spark's file source picks up:

wiki_to_files.py
import json, time, os, requests

URL = "https://stream.wikimedia.org/v2/stream/recentchange"
os.makedirs("stream_in", exist_ok=True)
headers = {"User-Agent": "AIMS-BDA-course/1.0 (student lab)", "Accept": "text/event-stream"}
buf, t0 = [], time.time()
with requests.get(URL, stream=True, headers=headers, timeout=60) as r:
    for line in r.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True):
        if line and line.startswith("data: "):
            buf.append(line[6:])
        if time.time() - t0 > 5 and buf:            # flush every 5 seconds
            with open(f"stream_in/{int(time.time()*1000)}.json", "w") as f:
                f.write("\n".join(buf))
            buf, t0 = [], time.time()

schema = "wiki string, type string, bot boolean, timestamp long, title string, user string"
edits = (spark.readStream.schema(schema).json("stream_in/")
         .withColumn("event_time", F.col("timestamp").cast("timestamp")))

per_wiki = (edits.withWatermark("event_time", "1 minute")
            .groupBy(F.window("event_time", "1 minute"), "wiki", "bot").count())
per_wiki.writeStream.outputMode("update").format("console").start()

docs.title: 9.6 Streaming algorithms: bounded memory, unbounded data
docs.text:
When you cannot store everything, use sketches — compact summaries with provable error bounds.

Problem Algorithm Memory Uniform sample of a stream Reservoir sampling \(O(k)\) Distinct count HyperLogLog ~KB for ~2% error Frequencies of items / heavy hitters Count-Min Sketch \(O(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\log\frac{1}{\delta})\) Quantiles t-digest, KLL ~KB Membership ("seen before?") Bloom filter bits per item

docs.title: Reservoir sampling (Algorithm R)
docs.text:
Keep the first \(k\) items; for the \(i\)-th item (\(i > k\)), replace a random reservoir slot with probability \(k/i\). Every item ends up in the sample with probability \(k/n\).

import random
def reservoir(stream, k, seed=0):
    rng = random.Random(seed); sample = []
    for i, x in enumerate(stream, 1):
        if i <= k: sample.append(x)
        else:
            j = rng.randint(1, i)
            if j <= k: sample[j - 1] = x
    return sample

docs.title: Count-Min Sketch
docs.text:
import numpy as np, hashlib
class CountMin:
    def __init__(self, width=2000, depth=5):
        self.w, self.d = width, depth
        self.table = np.zeros((depth, width), dtype=np.int64)
    def _h(self, x, i):
        return int(hashlib.blake2b(f"{i}:{x}".encode(), digest_size=8).hexdigest(), 16) % self.w
    def add(self, x, c=1):
        for i in range(self.d): self.table[i, self._h(x, i)] += c
    def estimate(self, x):
        return min(self.table[i, self._h(x, i)] for i in range(self.d))   # never underestimates

Spark has built-ins: F.approx_count_distinct (HyperLogLog++), percentile_approx, df.stat.countMinSketch, df.stat.bloomFilter.

docs.title: 10. Geospatial & satellite big data
docs.text:
Learning objectives

  • Distinguish vector and raster data and know their big data formats (GeoParquet, Cloud-Optimised GeoTIFF, Zarr).
  • Perform spatial joins and understand why they are expensive at scale.
  • Use hierarchical hexagonal indexing (H3) to turn spatial problems into fast table joins.
  • Process large climate/satellite rasters lazily with xarray + Dask.
  • Know the spatial extensions for big data engines: DuckDB spatial, Apache Sedona.

Geospatial data is among the most valuable big data for Africa: agriculture, climate adaptation, health access, urban planning and humanitarian response all depend on it.

docs.title: 10.1 Vector and raster
docs.text:
Vector Raster Model Points, lines, polygons with attributes Grid of cells (pixels) with values Examples Health facilities, roads (OpenStreetMap), district boundaries, building footprints Rainfall (CHIRPS), satellite imagery (Sentinel-2), population grids (WorldPop), elevation Big data formats GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf Cloud-Optimised GeoTIFF (COG), Zarr, NetCDF Python tools GeoPandas, Shapely, DuckDB spatial, Apache Sedona rasterio, rioxarray, xarray + Dask

Coordinate reference systems (CRS). Latitude/longitude (EPSG:4326) is in degrees — fine for storage, wrong for distances and areas. For Rwanda, project to UTM zone 35S (EPSG:32735) to measure metres.

docs.title: 10.2 GeoPandas basics
docs.text:
import geopandas as gpd

# Rwanda district boundaries (e.g., from geoBoundaries or HDX)
districts = gpd.read_file("data/rwa_adm2.geojson").to_crs(32735)
districts["area_km2"] = districts.area / 1e6
print(districts[["shapeName", "area_km2"]].sort_values("area_km2").head())

facilities = gpd.read_file("data/rwa_health_facilities.geojson").to_crs(32735)
joined = gpd.sjoin(facilities, districts[["shapeName", "geometry"]], predicate="within")
print(joined.groupby("shapeName").size().sort_values())

districts.to_parquet("data/rwa_adm2.parquet")      # GeoParquet

docs.title: 10.3 Why spatial joins are hard at scale
docs.text:
Naively testing every point against every polygon costs \(O(n \cdot m)\): 10 million buildings × 2,000 sectors = \(2\times10^{10}\) point-in-polygon tests. Systems use spatial indexes:

  • R-trees (GeoPandas sindex, PostGIS): bounding-box hierarchy; candidates first, exact test second.
  • Grid / space-filling curves (geohash, S2, H3): assign each geometry to cells; join on cell IDs — a regular equi-join that Spark, DuckDB and Polars do extremely well and that distributes across machines.

docs.title: 10.4 H3: hexagons for analytics
docs.text:
H3 (originally from Uber) divides the globe into hexagons at 16 resolutions. Each cell has a 64-bit ID, and IDs nest hierarchically.

Resolution Average cell area Use 5 ~250 km² Regional climate summaries 7 ~5 km² Sector-level analysis in Rwanda 8 ~0.7 km² Urban neighbourhoods 9 ~0.1 km² Street blocks

Hexagons have uniform neighbour distances (all 6 neighbours equidistant), which is better for smoothing and movement analysis than squares.

import h3   # version 4 API

kigali = (-1.9441, 30.0619)
cell = h3.latlng_to_cell(*kigali, 8)
print(cell, h3.cell_to_latlng(cell))
print(h3.grid_disk(cell, 1))           # cell plus its 6 neighbours
print(h3.cell_to_parent(cell, 5))      # coarser cell containing it
print(h3.cell_area(cell, unit="km^2"))

docs.title: Pattern: aggregate millions of points with H3 in DuckDB or Polars
docs.text:
import duckdb
con = duckdb.connect()
con.sql("INSTALL h3 FROM community; LOAD h3;")
con.sql("INSTALL spatial; LOAD spatial;")

# Buildings for Rwanda (e.g., Google Open Buildings CSV: latitude, longitude, area_in_meters, confidence)
con.sql("""
    CREATE TABLE b AS
    SELECT h3_latlng_to_cell(latitude, longitude, 8) AS h8, area_in_meters, confidence
    FROM read_csv_auto('data/open_buildings_rwanda/*.csv.gz')
    WHERE confidence >= 0.75
""")
con.sql("""
    SELECT h8, count(*) AS n_buildings, sum(area_in_meters) AS built_m2
    FROM b GROUP BY h8 ORDER BY n_buildings DESC LIMIT 10
""").show()

docs.title: H3 with Spark
docs.text:
import h3
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, types as T
import pandas as pd

@F.pandas_udf(T.StringType())
def to_h3(lat: pd.Series, lng: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    return pd.Series([h3.latlng_to_cell(a, b, 8) for a, b in zip(lat, lng)])

pts = spark.read.parquet("data/points.parquet").withColumn("h8", to_h3("lat", "lng"))

On Databricks, H3 functions are built into SQL (h3_longlatash3); Apache Sedona also provides H3 and full spatial SQL.

docs.title: 10.5 Spatial SQL at scale: DuckDB spatial and Apache Sedona
docs.text:
con.sql("""
    SELECT d.shapeName, count(*) AS n
    FROM ST_Read('data/rwa_adm2.geojson') d
    JOIN 'data/facilities.parquet' f
      ON ST_Contains(d.geom, ST_Point(f.lon, f.lat))
    GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC
""").show()

Apache Sedona adds spatial types, functions and spatially-partitioned joins to Spark:

from sedona.spark import SedonaContext
config = SedonaContext.builder().config(
    "spark.jars.packages",
    "org.apache.sedona:sedona-spark-shaded-<spark-version>_2.13:<sedona-version>").getOrCreate()
sedona = SedonaContext.create(config)

sedona.read.format("geoparquet").load("data/buildings.parquet").createOrReplaceTempView("b")
sedona.read.format("geoparquet").load("data/rwa_adm3.parquet").createOrReplaceTempView("s")
sedona.sql("""
    SELECT s.shapeName, count(*) AS n
    FROM s JOIN b ON ST_Contains(s.geometry, b.geometry)
    GROUP BY s.shapeName
""").show()

docs.title: 10.6 Raster big data with xarray and Dask
docs.text: Climate datasets are multi-dimensional arrays (time × latitude × longitude). xarray gives labelled arrays; with chunks=, it uses Dask to process data larger than memory lazily.

docs.title: Example: CHIRPS rainfall over Rwanda
docs.text:
CHIRPS provides daily rainfall at 0.05° (~5 km) for 1981–present. The examples use CHIRPS v2.0 file names; the Climate Hazards Center has been rolling out CHIRPS v3, so check the portal and adjust paths if you use the newer version.

import xarray as xr

# Download yearly global daily files (≈1 GB each) from the CHC data portal, e.g.
# https://data.chc.ucsb.edu/products/CHIRPS-2.0/global_daily/netcdf/p05/chirps-v2.0.2023.days_p05.nc
ds = xr.open_mfdataset("data/chirps/chirps-v2.0.*.days_p05.nc",
                       chunks={"time": 365}, combine="by_coords")

rw = ds.precip.sel(latitude=slice(-2.9, -1.0), longitude=slice(28.8, 30.95))   # Rwanda bbox

monthly = rw.resample(time="MS").sum()                      # lazy
clim = monthly.groupby("time.month").mean("time")           # monthly climatology
anom = monthly.groupby("time.month") - clim                 # anomalies
season_a = monthly.sel(time=monthly.time.dt.month.isin([9, 10, 11, 12]))  # Sept–Dec rains

clim.compute().plot(col="month", col_wrap=4, cmap="Blues")

docs.title: Clip to district boundaries and summarise
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
import rioxarray  # noqa: F401  (adds .rio accessor)
annual = rw.resample(time="YS").sum().rio.write_crs(4326).rio.set_spatial_dims(
    x_dim="longitude", y_dim="latitude")

districts4326 = districts.to_crs(4326)
rows = []
for _, d in districts4326.iterrows():
    clipped = annual.rio.clip([d.geometry], all_touched=True)
    s = clipped.mean(["latitude", "longitude"]).to_series()
    rows.append(s.rename(d.shapeName))
district_rain = pd.concat(rows, axis=1)     # years × districts

docs.title: Satellite imagery: Cloud-Optimised GeoTIFFs and STAC
docs.text:
Modern imagery archives (Sentinel-2, Landsat, Digital Earth Africa) store COGs in object storage and catalogue them with STAC (SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog). You query the catalogue, then read only the pixels you need over HTTP.

# pip install pystac-client odc-stac
from pystac_client import Client
import odc.stac

catalog = Client.open("https://explorer.digitalearth.africa/stac")
items = catalog.search(collections=["s2_l2a"], bbox=[30.0, -2.0, 30.2, -1.9],
                       datetime="2024-06-01/2024-08-31",
                       query={"eo:cloud_cover": {"lt": 20}}).item_collection()
cube = odc.stac.load(items, bands=["red", "nir"], resolution=10, chunks={"x": 2048, "y": 2048})
ndvi = (cube.nir - cube.red) / (cube.nir + cube.red)        # vegetation index, lazy
ndvi.median("time").compute().plot(cmap="RdYlGn", vmin=0, vmax=0.8)

Access requirements

Digital Earth Africa's data is public in AWS (af-south-1, Cape Town). Some readers need AWS_NO_SIGN_REQUEST=YES set in the environment. Check the DE Africa documentation for current endpoints and collection names.

docs.title: 11. Text & graph analytics at scale
docs.text:
Learning objectives

  • Build scalable text pipelines: tokenisation, TF-IDF, hashing trick, topic models.
  • Find near-duplicate documents with MinHash and Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH).
  • Represent large graphs and compute degree, PageRank and connected components in a distributed way.
  • Apply these methods to African-language text and to networks such as mobility or transactions.

docs.title: 11.1 From text to vectors
docs.text:
Text is the largest unstructured data source: web pages, social media, SMS, call-centre transcripts, parliamentary records. The classic scalable pipeline:

flowchart LR
    D[Raw documents] --> T[Tokenise] --> S[Remove stop words] --> N[n-grams] --> V[Vectorise:<br/>counts / hashing] --> W[Weight: TF-IDF] --> M[Model: classify,<br/>cluster, topics, search]

TF-IDF weights a term \(t\) in document \(d\) by how frequent it is in \(d\) and how rare across the \(N\) documents:

\[ \text{tfidf}(t,d) = \text{tf}(t,d)\cdot \log\frac{N+1}{\text{df}(t)+1}. \]

Computing \(\text{df}(t)\) needs a pass over the whole corpus — a word count (Chapter 4).

The hashing trick. A vocabulary of millions of words needs a large dictionary shared by all workers. Instead, map each token to hash(token) mod 2^k — no dictionary, no extra pass, fixed memory. Collisions are rare enough with \(2^{18}\)–\(2^{20}\) features.

docs.title: 11.2 Spark ML text pipeline
docs.text:
from pyspark.ml import Pipeline
from pyspark.ml.feature import RegexTokenizer, StopWordsRemover, HashingTF, IDF, NGram
from pyspark.ml.classification import LogisticRegression
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

reviews = spark.read.json("data/amazon_reviews/*.jsonl.gz")      # e.g. Amazon Reviews 2023
data = (reviews.select("text", "rating")
        .withColumn("label", (F.col("rating") >= 4).cast("double"))
        .filter(F.length("text") > 20))

tok = RegexTokenizer(inputCol="text", outputCol="tokens", pattern=r"\W+", minTokenLength=2)
sw  = StopWordsRemover(inputCol="tokens", outputCol="words")
tf  = HashingTF(inputCol="words", outputCol="tf", numFeatures=2**18)
idf = IDF(inputCol="tf", outputCol="features", minDocFreq=5)
clf = LogisticRegression(maxIter=30, regParam=0.01)

model = Pipeline(stages=[tok, sw, tf, idf, clf]).fit(data)

StopWordsRemover ships lists for several languages (StopWordsRemover.loadDefaultStopWords("french")). For Kinyarwanda and many other African languages there is no built-in list: build one from corpus frequency (top-N most frequent tokens, reviewed by a speaker) — a good exercise in itself.

docs.title: 11.3 Topic modelling with LDA
docs.text:
from pyspark.ml.feature import CountVectorizer
from pyspark.ml.clustering import LDA

cv = CountVectorizer(inputCol="words", outputCol="counts", vocabSize=20000, minDF=10)
cv_model = cv.fit(words_df); counts = cv_model.transform(words_df)
lda = LDA(k=15, maxIter=20, featuresCol="counts").fit(counts)

vocab = cv_model.vocabulary
for row in lda.describeTopics(8).collect():
    print(row.topic, [vocab[i] for i in row.termIndices])

docs.title: 11.4 Near-duplicate detection: MinHash and LSH
docs.text:
Web crawls and news feeds contain many near-copies. Comparing all pairs of \(n\) documents is \(O(n^2)\) — impossible for \(10^8\) documents.

  1. Represent each document as a set of shingles (e.g., word 3-grams).
  2. Jaccard similarity \(J(A,B) = |A\cap B| / |A\cup B|\).
  3. MinHash: for a random hash function \(h\), \(\Pr[\min h(A) = \min h(B)] = J(A,B)\). A signature of \(k\) min-hashes estimates \(J\).
  4. LSH: split signatures into bands; documents sharing any identical band become candidate pairs. Only candidates are compared.
from pyspark.ml.feature import MinHashLSH, NGram, HashingTF

ng = NGram(n=3, inputCol="words", outputCol="shingles")
htf = HashingTF(inputCol="shingles", outputCol="sh_vec", numFeatures=2**20, binary=True)
docs = htf.transform(ng.transform(words_df)).filter(F.size("shingles") > 0)

mh = MinHashLSH(inputCol="sh_vec", outputCol="hashes", numHashTables=5).fit(docs)
pairs = mh.approxSimilarityJoin(docs, docs, threshold=0.3, distCol="jaccard_dist") \
          .filter("datasetA.id < datasetB.id")

docs.title: 11.5 Beyond bag-of-words
docs.text: Transformer embeddings (multilingual models such as AfroXLMR, Serengeti, or general multilingual sentence encoders) capture meaning far better. At scale, the pattern is the same as model scoring in Chapter 8: broadcast or load the model once per executor and embed in batches with a pandas UDF; store vectors in Parquet; search with an approximate nearest-neighbour index (FAISS, or the vector functions in DuckDB/Lance). GPU access usually becomes the constraint, not data size.

docs.title: 11.6 Graph basics
docs.text:
A graph \(G = (V, E)\): people and calls, accounts and transfers, web pages and links, road intersections and segments. Big graphs have billions of edges and power-law degree distributions: a few hubs with enormous degree (skew, again!).

Representations for distributed processing:

  • Edge list table (src, dst, weight) — the natural format for Spark and DuckDB.
  • Adjacency lists (node, [neighbours]) — good for iterative message passing.

NetworkX is excellent up to ~1 million edges; beyond that, use distributed or optimised engines (GraphFrames on Spark, or single-node libraries such as igraph and graph-tool).

docs.title: 11.7 Degree and triangles with plain DataFrames
docs.text:
edges = spark.read.parquet("data/edges.parquet")    # src, dst
deg = (edges.select(F.col("src").alias("node")).union(edges.select(F.col("dst").alias("node")))
       .groupBy("node").count().withColumnRenamed("count", "degree"))
deg.orderBy(F.desc("degree")).show(10)

# Degree distribution on log–log scale reveals power laws
dist = deg.groupBy("degree").count().toPandas()

docs.title: 11.8 PageRank as iterated MapReduce
docs.text:
PageRank models a random surfer who follows links with probability \(d\) (≈0.85) and teleports otherwise:

\[ PR(v) = \frac{1-d}{N} + d \sum_{u \to v} \frac{PR(u)}{\text{out}(u)}. \]

Each iteration is one map (each node sends \(PR(u)/\text{out}(u)\) to its neighbours) and one reduce (sum incoming contributions) — a join plus a groupBy.

from pyspark.sql import functions as F
N = edges.select("src").union(edges.select("dst")).distinct().count()
out_deg = edges.groupBy("src").agg(F.count("*").alias("out"))
links = edges.join(out_deg, "src").cache()

ranks = links.select(F.col("src").alias("node")).union(links.select(F.col("dst").alias("node"))) \
             .distinct().withColumn("pr", F.lit(1.0 / N))
d = 0.85
for i in range(15):
    contrib = (links.join(ranks.withColumnRenamed("node", "src"), "src")
               .select(F.col("dst").alias("node"), (F.col("pr") / F.col("out")).alias("c")))
    ranks = (contrib.groupBy("node").agg(F.sum("c").alias("s"))
             .select("node", ((1 - d) / N + d * F.col("s")).alias("pr")))
    if i % 5 == 4:
        ranks = ranks.localCheckpoint()     # truncate lineage growth in long loops
ranks.orderBy(F.desc("pr")).show(10)

(Dangling nodes with no out-links leak rank in this simple version; production implementations redistribute it.)

docs.title: 12. Pipelines, orchestration & the cloud
docs.text:
Learning objectives

  • Design ETL/ELT pipelines with layered (medallion) architecture.
  • Write idempotent, testable pipeline steps with data quality checks.
  • Explain workflow orchestration (DAGs, scheduling, retries, backfills) with Apache Airflow.
  • Package environments with Docker for reproducibility.
  • Compare cloud big data services and estimate costs.

docs.title: 12.1 From notebook to pipeline
docs.text:
A notebook answers a question once. A pipeline answers it every day, reliably, without you. Properties of a good pipeline:

Property Meaning How Idempotent Re-running gives the same result, no duplicates Overwrite partitions by date; MERGE instead of blind append Incremental Processes only new data Partition by ingestion date; track watermarks/offsets Observable You know when and why it fails Logging, metrics, alerts Tested Code and data are checked Unit tests on functions; data quality assertions Reproducible Same inputs + code → same outputs Version control, pinned environments, containers

docs.title: 12.2 ETL vs ELT and the medallion architecture
docs.text:
• ETL (Extract–Transform–Load): transform before loading into a warehouse. Traditional.
  • ELT: load raw data first into cheap storage, transform inside the lake/warehouse engine. Modern default, because storage is cheap and raw data can be reprocessed when logic changes.
flowchart LR
    SRC[Sources:<br/>APIs, files, DBs, streams] --> B[(Bronze<br/>raw, as received<br/>append-only)]
    B --> S[(Silver<br/>cleaned, typed,<br/>deduplicated, joined)]
    S --> G[(Gold<br/>aggregates & features<br/>for dashboards / ML)]
pipeline/steps.py
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, functions as F

def bronze_to_silver(raw: DataFrame) -> DataFrame:
    return (raw
        .withColumn("pickup_ts", F.to_timestamp("tpep_pickup_datetime"))
        .withColumn("dropoff_ts", F.to_timestamp("tpep_dropoff_datetime"))
        .filter(F.col("fare_amount").between(0, 1000))
        .filter(F.col("dropoff_ts") > F.col("pickup_ts"))
        .dropDuplicates(["VendorID", "pickup_ts", "dropoff_ts", "PULocationID", "DOLocationID"])
        .withColumn("ds", F.to_date("pickup_ts")))

def silver_to_gold(silver: DataFrame) -> DataFrame:
    return (silver.groupBy("ds", "PULocationID")
            .agg(F.count("*").alias("trips"), F.sum("total_amount").alias("revenue")))

Idempotent writes of one day's partition:

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode", "dynamic")
(silver_to_gold(silver.filter(F.col("ds") == run_date))
   .write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("ds").parquet("lake/gold/zone_daily"))

docs.title: Unit tests with a small Spark session
Data quality checks
docs.text:
Write assertions about the data itself: row counts within expected ranges, no nulls in keys, valid ranges, referential integrity, freshness.

def check(df, run_date):
    problems = []
    n = df.count()
    if n == 0: problems.append("no rows")
    nulls = df.filter(F.col("PULocationID").isNull()).count()
    if nulls / max(n, 1) > 0.01: problems.append(f"{nulls} null zones")
    if df.filter(F.col("trips") < 0).count(): problems.append("negative counts")
    if problems:
        raise ValueError(f"DQ failed for {run_date}: {problems}")

Libraries such as Great Expectations, Soda and pandera (pandas/Polars/PySpark schemas) formalise this.

docs.title: 12.4 Orchestration with Apache Airflow
docs.text:
An orchestrator runs pipeline steps in the right order, on a schedule, with retries, alerts and backfills (re-running past dates). In Airflow, a workflow is a DAG of tasks defined in Python.

dags/taxi_daily.py
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from airflow.sdk import dag, task        # Airflow 3 TaskFlow API (Airflow 2: from airflow.decorators import dag, task)

@dag(schedule="@daily", start_date=datetime(2024, 1, 1), catchup=False,
     default_args={"retries": 2, "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=10)}, tags=["aims-bda"])
def taxi_daily():

    @task
    def ingest(ds=None):
        # download / land raw files for date ds into bronze
        ...

    @task
    def to_silver(ds=None):
        # spark-submit pipeline/jobs/silver.py --date ds
        ...

    @task
    def to_gold(ds=None): ...

    @task
    def quality(ds=None): ...

    ingest() >> to_silver() >> to_gold() >> quality()

taxi_daily()

Alternatives worth knowing: Prefect and Dagster (Python-native, asset-oriented), dbt (SQL transformations with tests and lineage inside a warehouse or DuckDB), and cloud-managed schedulers (Databricks Workflows, AWS Step Functions, Google Cloud Composer).

docs.title: 13. Ethics, privacy & governance
docs.text:
Learning objectives

  • Identify ethical risks across the big data lifecycle: collection, linkage, modelling, deployment.
  • Explain why anonymisation is hard and how re-identification happens.
  • Apply k-anonymity and differential privacy to datasets and queries.
  • Summarise the key obligations of Rwanda's personal data protection law and related African frameworks.
  • Audit a model for performance gaps across groups.

docs.title: 13.1 Why big data raises new ethical problems
docs.text:
Big data changes the scale and nature of harm:

  • Linkage. Individually harmless datasets (mobile phone location, mobile money, social media) become revealing when joined.
  • Inference. Models infer sensitive attributes (health, ethnicity, income, sexual orientation) that were never collected.
  • Scale of error. A biased rule applied to one million loan applicants harms at scale.
  • Power asymmetry. Those who hold the data — governments, telecoms, platforms, often foreign — know far more than those described by it.
  • Representation. Data from smartphones and the internet under-represents rural, older, poorer and female populations in many African countries; "big" data is not "complete" data.

docs.title: 13.2 The myth of anonymous data
docs.text:
Removing names is not anonymisation. Classic results:

  • Sweeney (2000) estimated that 87% of the US population is uniquely identified by ZIP code + gender + date of birth.
  • de Montjoye et al. (2013) showed that four spatio-temporal points are enough to uniquely identify 95% of individuals in a mobile phone dataset of 1.5 million people.
  • de Montjoye et al. (2015) found similar results for credit card transactions.

Attributes that are not identifiers alone but identify in combination are quasi-identifiers.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_parquet("survey.parquet")
qi = ["district", "sex", "age", "occupation"]
group_sizes = df.groupby(qi).size()
print("share of people unique on QIs:", (group_sizes == 1).sum() / len(df))

docs.title: 13.3 k-anonymity
docs.text:
A dataset is k-anonymous if every combination of quasi-identifier values appears at least \(k\) times. Achieve it by:

  • generalisation — age 34 → 30–39; village → district;
  • suppression — remove rare records or values.
def k_anonymity(df, qi):
    return df.groupby(qi, observed=True).size().min()

df["age_band"] = pd.cut(df.age, bins=[0, 18, 30, 45, 60, 120], right=False)
print(k_anonymity(df, ["district", "sex", "age"]))        # often 1
print(k_anonymity(df, ["province", "sex", "age_band"]))   # much larger

Limitations: k-anonymity is vulnerable when all records in a group share the same sensitive value (homogeneity attack) — addressed by l-diversity and t-closeness — and it offers no guarantee against attackers with auxiliary data.

docs.title: 13.4 Differential privacy
docs.text:
Differential privacy (DP) is a mathematical guarantee about an algorithm, not a dataset. A randomised mechanism \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-differentially private if for all datasets \(D, D'\) differing in one person, and all outputs \(S\),

\[ \Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon}\,\Pr[M(D') \in S]. \]

Intuition: the output is almost equally likely whether or not you are in the data, so it reveals little about you. Smaller \(\varepsilon\) → more privacy, more noise.

docs.title: The Laplace mechanism
docs.text:
For a query \(f\) with sensitivity \(\Delta f = \max |f(D) - f(D')|\), release \(f(D) + \text{Laplace}(0, \Delta f/\varepsilon)\). A count has sensitivity 1.

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def dp_count(true_count, epsilon):
    return true_count + rng.laplace(0, 1 / epsilon)

def dp_mean(x, lower, upper, epsilon):
    x = np.clip(x, lower, upper)
    # split budget between sum and count
    s = x.sum() + rng.laplace(0, (upper - lower) / (epsilon / 2))
    n = len(x) + rng.laplace(0, 1 / (epsilon / 2))
    return s / max(n, 1)

true = 1234
for eps in (0.01, 0.1, 1, 10):
    print(eps, [round(dp_count(true, eps)) for _ in range(5)])

Key properties:

  • Composition. Answering queries with budgets \(\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_k\) costs \(\sum \varepsilon_i\) in total. Privacy is a budget you spend.
  • Post-processing. Anything computed from a DP output remains DP.
  • Group size matters. Noise of ±10 is negligible for a district count of 50,000 and destructive for a village of 30.

The US Census Bureau used DP for the 2020 census; tools include OpenDP and Google's DP libraries, and Tumult Analytics (which runs on Spark).

docs.title: 13.5 Fairness and bias
docs.text: Bias enters at every stage: who is in the data (sampling), how labels were produced (historical discrimination), which features proxy for protected attributes (location often proxies for ethnicity or income), and how predictions are used.

docs.title: Group performance audit
docs.text:
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, recall_score
def audit(df, group, y="label", p="score", thr=0.5):
    rows = []
    for g, d in df.groupby(group):
        rows.append({group: g, "n": len(d), "base_rate": d[y].mean(),
                     "auc": roc_auc_score(d[y], d[p]) if d[y].nunique() > 1 else np.nan,
                     "tpr": recall_score(d[y], d[p] >= thr),
                     "flag_rate": (d[p] >= thr).mean()})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

print(audit(scored_pdf, "urban_rural"))

Common fairness criteria — demographic parity (equal flag rates), equal opportunity (equal TPR), calibration within groups — cannot all hold at once when base rates differ (Kleinberg et al. 2016; Chouldechova 2017). Choosing among them is a value judgement that must involve affected communities, not only data scientists.

docs.title: 13.6 The legal landscape
docs.text:
Not legal advice

This section is an educational summary. Laws and regulations change; for real projects, consult the official texts, the supervisory authority's guidance, and your institution's legal or ethics office.

docs.title: Rwanda: Law No. 058/2021 on the protection of personal data and privacy
docs.text:
Rwanda's law, published in October 2021 and fully applicable after a two-year transition, follows principles similar to the EU's GDPR. Key points for data scientists:

  • Supervisory authority: the National Cyber Security Authority (NCSA). Data controllers and processors must register with it.
  • Principles: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality; accountability.
  • Lawful bases for processing include consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public interest and legitimate interests.
  • Sensitive personal data (for example health, genetic and biometric data, ethnic or social origin, religious or political beliefs, sexual life, criminal records) faces stricter conditions.
  • Data subject rights include access, rectification, erasure, objection, data portability, and not being subject to decisions based solely on automated processing with significant effects.
  • Data breaches must be notified to the authority promptly (the law sets a short deadline, measured in hours), and to affected persons where there is high risk.
  • Storage and transfer outside Rwanda are restricted: storing personal data outside Rwanda requires authorisation from the NCSA, and cross-border transfers need an adequate legal basis or safeguards.
  • Data protection impact assessments are expected for high-risk processing — large-scale profiling and big data projects often qualify.

Implications for your projects: before using phone, health, financial or survey microdata, establish the legal basis, minimise and pseudonymise, check where cloud storage physically resides, document a DPIA, and obtain ethics approval (e.g., from your institution's research ethics committee, and the Rwanda National Ethics Committee for health research).

docs.title: Wider frameworks
docs.text:
• African Union Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection (Malabo Convention, adopted 2014, in force since 2023).
  • AU Data Policy Framework (2022) — promotes data flows within Africa alongside protection and sovereignty.
  • National laws across the continent, e.g., Kenya's Data Protection Act (2019), Nigeria's Data Protection Act (2023), South Africa's POPIA.
  • EU GDPR applies when processing data of people in the EU — relevant for international collaborations.
  • Rwanda's national policies on data (e.g., the Data Revolution Policy) and on artificial intelligence (National AI Policy) set the government's direction on open data, sharing and responsible AI.

docs.title: 13.7 Governance in practice
docs.text:
Practice What it means Data inventory and classification Know what you hold; label public / internal / personal / sensitive Access control Least privilege; role-based access; audit logs Pseudonymisation Replace identifiers with keyed hashes (HMAC with a secret key — plain hashes of phone numbers are reversible by brute force) Retention Delete data when its purpose ends; lakehouse DELETE + VACUUM makes this feasible Lineage and documentation Datasheets for datasets, model cards for models Open data with care Publish aggregates with suppression or DP, not microdata 
import hmac, hashlib, os
SECRET = os.environ["PSEUDO_KEY"].encode()      # store in a secrets manager, never in code
def pseudonymise(msisdn: str) -> str:
    return hmac.new(SECRET, msisdn.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()[:16]

docs.title: 13.8 Case studies for discussion
docs.text:
1. Mobile phone data for poverty mapping. Studies (e.g., Blumenstock, Cadamuro & On, Science, 2015 — using Rwandan phone data) predicted wealth from call records. Discuss: consent, benefit to subscribers, risk of misuse, accuracy for people without phones.
  2. Mobility data during COVID-19. Aggregated mobility statistics guided lockdown policy in several African countries. What aggregation and governance made this acceptable? What could go wrong?
  3. Credit scoring from smartphone data. Digital lenders in East Africa score borrowers from phone metadata. Discuss transparency, the right not to be subject to automated decisions, and debt-collection practices.
  4. Satellite imagery and privacy. Building-level mapping supports planning and disaster response, but can also enable surveillance or eviction. Where is the line?

docs.title: Synthetic data (when real data is sensitive)
docs.text:
When real data involves personal information, generate synthetic data with realistic structure:

  • PaySim (on Kaggle): synthetic mobile money transactions based on an African mobile money service — fraud detection, graph motifs.
  • Faker + your own generator: produce millions of realistic records (names, districts, timestamps) for streaming labs.
  • Synthea: synthetic patient health records.

fake = Faker()
districts = ["Gasabo", "Kicukiro", "Nyarugenge", "Huye", "Musanze", "Rubavu", "Nyagatare", "Rusizi"]

    return {"txn_id": fake.uuid4(), "sender": fake.msisdn()[:10], "receiver": fake.msisdn()[:10],

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Action A Spark operation that triggers execution and returns a result or writes output (count, collect, write). Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) Spark feature that re-optimises a query at runtime using statistics from completed stages. Amdahl's law The maximum speed-up from parallelism is limited by the serial fraction of a program: \(S = 1/((1-p) + p/N)\). Apache Arrow A standard in-memory columnar data format enabling zero-copy data sharing between tools and languages. Broadcast join Join strategy where a small table is copied to every worker, avoiding a shuffle of the large table. CAP theorem During a network partition, a distributed data store must choose between consistency and availability. Checkpoint Saved state (offsets, aggregation state) that allows a streaming query to recover after failure; also used to truncate long lineage. Combiner A local reduce applied to map output before the shuffle to reduce data transfer. Columnar storage Storing each column contiguously; efficient for analytical queries that read few columns. Data lake / Lakehouse A data lake stores raw files in cheap object storage; a lakehouse adds a transaction log (Delta Lake, Iceberg, Hudi) for ACID tables on top. DAG Directed acyclic graph — the plan of tasks and dependencies built by Spark, Dask or an orchestrator. Differential privacy A mathematical privacy guarantee that an algorithm's output changes little whether or not any one person's data is included. Driver / Executor In Spark, the driver plans and schedules work; executors run tasks on partitions. Event time / Processing time When an event happened versus when the system processed it. H3 A hierarchical hexagonal global grid system for spatial indexing. Idempotent An operation that gives the same result when repeated; essential for retries and backfills. Lazy evaluation Deferring computation until a result is required, allowing whole-plan optimisation. Lineage The record of transformations that produced a dataset; Spark uses it to recompute lost partitions. MapReduce A programming model where computation is expressed as map and reduce functions, with the framework handling distribution, shuffling and failures. Mergeable statistic A statistic whose partial results on subsets combine exactly into the result on the whole (sum, count, mean via sum and count, variance via Chan's formula). Parquet An open columnar file format with encoding, compression and per-chunk statistics. Partition (1) A chunk of a distributed dataset processed by one task. (2) A directory in a partitioned dataset (year=2024/). (3) A network split in the CAP theorem. (4) A shard of a Kafka topic. Predicate / projection pushdown Applying filters (predicates) and column selection (projection) at the data source to read less data. Shuffle Redistribution of data across workers by key; required for wide operations like groupBy and join. Skew Uneven distribution of data across keys/partitions, causing a few slow tasks. Sketch A compact probabilistic summary of a data stream (HyperLogLog, Count-Min, t-digest). Transformation A lazy Spark operation that defines a new dataset from an existing one (select, filter, join). Watermark A threshold on event time that tells a streaming engine how long to wait for late data before finalising results.
